subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. In view of the anxiety being expressed throughout the country by Indian organizations and other spokesmen for the Indian people, including the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras), about the failure of the government to consult the Indian people before proceeding with the reorganization of the department of Indian affairs will he undertake to reconsider these proposals in consultation with representatives of the Indian community in Canada?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as this house knows there has been constant and intense communication with the Indian population since this government took office on all aspects concerning the Indian population. The reorganization of the department is something which had been initiated quite a while ago. It is just a matter of internal structure, and the obvious design is to make the services of the government to the Indian and Eskimo population more efficient. It is really a consequence of Indian Affairs being no longer just a branch but being a whole department; because it was a matter of internal reorganization we did not feel it was necessary to advise the Indians in advance of the day that it was going to take place.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION
speechtext: As a supplementary question, will the Prime Minister state whether, before proceeding with this reorganization, the government did or did not consult with the national and regional Indian advisory councils, which I understand were established by the government for precisely this purpose of consultation.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that both Mr. Chretien and Mr. Andras have been discussing this general idea amongst themselves and with the people concerned, but
they will have to answer for themselves when they are in the house. I have no specific information on that.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION
speechtext: As a further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, is the Prime Minister inclined to meet with representatives of the Indian Brotherhood of Canada, which organization has strongly protested this reorganization and demanded a meeting with the Prime Minister to discuss the matter?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not considered that yet. I have not received this invitation. I do not know of it, but I am inclined to believe that the minister and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) are very expert and able at this, and that whatever they have decided is a good decision.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION
speechtext:

supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that representatives of the Indian people have made it clear that they consider this reorganization more than an internal housekeeping affair, would the Prime Minister give consideration, first of all, to tabling the details of the reorganization and, second, referring the matter to the appropriate standing committee so that representatives of the Indian people could make public their observations and their criticisms of this plan?

the second reading of Bill No. S-2, to amend the Publication of Statutes Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, to begin with I should like to review for the house the history of this bill in the previous session of parliament. It was first introduced in the other place in 1967 during the course of the last parliament. It had been given second reading in the other chamber, considered there by the standing committee on banking and commerce, given third reading and passed, whereupon it reached this house in the spring of this year.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING FORM OF PRINTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I wonder whether copies of the bill could be distributed to our desks before we proceed with it. I know we have copies upstairs but we do not have them here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING FORM OF PRINTING
speechtext:
I think it is being distributed now, Mr. Speaker; the bill is at the table.
I was saying that last spring, just before parliament dissolved, the bill was introduced into this chamber. It was given first reading but debate on second reading had not been concluded at the time the house was dissolved.
A week or so ago the bill was introduced once more in the other place; it was given second reading and sent to the standing committee on banking and commerce. Certain technical amendments were made to it in the other place and the bill was given third reading. The text that hon. members now have before them incorporates the amendments made to the original bill by the Senate. I might say that those amendments are accepted by the government and the bill is now before this house for second reading.
The purpose of the bill is to give the governor in council authority to publish the statutes in a certain form. At the present time, as
Publication of Statutes Act members know, under the existing Publication of Statutes Act, the statutes must be published in separate volumes, in English and in French. The purpose of this bill is to enable the government to publish the statutes in another form, having the English and French texts in adjacent columns on the same page, thereby putting both versions of the statutes in the same volume. By courtesy of the house leaders of all parties, Mr. Speaker, bills have until today been submitted to this chamber in that form. Therefore Bill S-2 itself, which we are now discussing, appears in a form similar to that which would be provided for under the regulations by the governor in council should the house adopt this bill.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The Revised Statutes of Canada to be published in the course of the coming year will be printed in the form recommended by the commission on the revision of statutes and it is the intention that the revised statutes be in both languages, printed on the same page in parallel columns, thereby including both languages in the same volume. Since the revised statutes will be in this form the government feels it would be appropriate to publish the annual statutes in the same form.
For the information of all members the Clerk has at his table specimen copies of the revised statutes as they will appear when published, and hon. members who wish to see them could perhaps call at the table, or possibly the pages can distribute copies to those who are interested.
The reason for the introduction of this bill is that while section 133 of the British North America Act provides that the laws of Canada shall be published in both languages it does not provide that they should be published side by side. As a matter of fact, they have been published until now in separate volumes, one in English and the other in French. The intention now is to publish the two versions in the same volume. I believe this will prove to be a convenience in a number of ways. I believe the legal profession itself will derive benefit from the change.
I should like to recall to hon. members of this house learned in the law that the rules adopted by the courts in the interpretation of statutes provide that a statute in one language, if of doubtful interpretation, may be compared with the same statute in the other official language. In 1935, in the case of The King v. Dubois, the Supreme Court of Canada held that the two versions of a statute
October 1, 1968

Publication of Statutes Act must be read together and that the meaning in one case might be limited or extended by the corresponding words in the other version. In the province of Quebec the statutes are already printed in parallel columns, first in French and then in English. In 1937 the Quebec Superior Court in the case of Robitaille v. Beaupre upheld the proposition that where one version of a statute is susceptible to a meaning different from the other version, the version most consistent with the intention of the legislation should prevail.
I am suggesting it will be a great convenience to the bench, to members of the bar and to people generally to find both versions of a statute printed on the same page in the same volume, each casting light, meaning and interpretation one upon the other. I think I would be remiss if I failed to mention the feeling of the government and, I hope, of this house, that if we are to talk in terms of the equality of both official languages in Canada we should not limit ourselves to section 133 of the British North America Act. If we are to mean what we say, French speaking Canadians should be made to feel at home not only in Quebec but in other parts of the country, and have equal access to the law in their own language. The act of placing each version in parallel columns grants equality to the languages used. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said before the Senate committee last year when he was Minister of Justice, having two versions separate but equal, that is to say, in separate volumes, is not the same as having them equal and in the same volume. There should be equal access to each version in the same volume.
I was present during the last debate on this subject and listened with great interest to what was said by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner).

Having heard that speech, as well as the speech made on that occasion by the former hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, Mr. Churchill, I realize that some concern is felt about the additional cost of the new volumes and the size it is anticipated they may reach. When we reach the committee stage, if the house allows us to proceed, I believe I should be able to demonstrate that the cost will not be appreciably


greater than the current cost of producing these volumes, that the price paid by purchasers will not be appreciably more, and that the size of the volumes will not be appreciably increased. In other words, we intend that the volumes should be of a convenient size to carry into a court. We do not contemplate a cumbersome type of binding or printing.
I do not intend to deal with the amendments made in the Senate unless this matter is brought up during the committee stage. I shall simply add a few remarks having to do with the publication of statutes generally and the possibility of accelerating the speed with which these statutes can be published and revised. I think this is related to the larger area of legal reform, of bringing the law up to date with technology and the introduction of a greater degree of computerization in connection with the publication of the statutes in permanent form. I would think that the availability of the statutes in the two languages would enhance this possibility. Since 1960 much has been said and written in this area and today studies on these lines rank as a highly specialized discipline called jurimet-rics. I have had something to say about this outside the house but so far I have had no opportunity to mention it here.

Mr. Chairman, before clause 2 carries I would like to say one or two words. It seems to me there is nothing wrong with
Publication of Statutes Act the bill and it is very hard to oppose this type of legislation. I had the opportunity of participating in the move to get rid of one section of the statutes that most members of parliament never saw. There used to be another section attached to the statutes that one could order privately each year if one wished. With the deletion of that section I suppose we now have a little more money for printing statutes, but I wonder whether this is not really looking ahead to something else.
The idea of printing both language versions side by side may be all right but it is something that does not apply to very many people. I am sure that those who wish to conduct their business in the French language probably do so in toto and those who wish to conduct their business in English do so in toto.
Except in the rarified field of appeals there does not seem to be much use for this step. In instances of appeals lawyers may discuss the interpretation of a particular phrase in both languages. They may even go further than that and look into the interpretation given by the legislature when passing the bill, but in the main both versions are not going to be used. It seems to me that this step is a sop, more than anything else, to an expression of opinion widely prevalent in Canada today to this effect: Let us do something that is not really going to do anything, but nobody is really opposed to it.
If this bill really means what is says, providing for universality of both official languages in our statutes, then it seems to me that the courts will have to give some consideration to this matter. When I go over to Hull in the province of Quebec to pay a parking ticket or a fine for going through a light, since the law there is different from what it is in Ontario the court proceedings are conducted entirely in French and I do not know what is going on. I have had this experience personally. I have stood in the prisoners' dock, or whatever it may be, but I have not required the statute covering the offence. In any case it was probably a provincial statute. Therefore the usefulness of this proposal to the individual is going to be limited.
This may apply only to courts but it raises the whole problem of bilingualism. If the statutes in future must be in both languages I will need a knowledge of both languages, and it is time the federal government gave consideration to moving forward with a national education program that would make it possible for the average person to read the statutes in both languages. This is not possible for the average person now; yet we do not
October 1, 1968

Publication of Statutes Act seem to be moving in that direction. I know the minister may say that this is not a federal matter at the present time, but if we do not make it a federal matter printing the statutes in both languages will not mean much.
I am sure many people will be able to understand the French and English versions simultaneously, but I am doubtful that many will be able to understand them well enough to arrive at a fine point of interpretation in making an argument. High school education in Ontario will not give a person that understanding of the other language, and so I suggest that we are in a way putting the horse behind the cart rather than in front of it.
If Canada is to become a bilingual nation, and if it is the intention of the government that it become so, then I hope this is only a beginning and that we will set about making it possible for this form of printing the statutes to be of some use to at least 75 per cent of Canadians who have no use for it now.

speechtext:

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize and provide for the construction of a line of railway in the province of Alberta by Canadian National Railway Company from the vicinity of Windfall on the Windfall extension to the Sangudo subdivision on the Canadian National Railway in a westerly direction for a distance of approximately 51 miles to the Bigstone property of Pan American Petroleum Corporation and of a connecting spur extending in a northerly direction for a distance of approximately 9 miles to the South Kaybob property of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited and its associates at a total expenditure of $10,435,000, not to be exceeded by more than 15 per cent.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Faulkner in the chair.

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF ALBERTA BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a resolution preceding a bill to enable the
[Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) .1
DEBATES	October 1, 1968
Canadian National Railway Company to complete approximately 60 miles of new branch line trackage to serve the requirements of two new sulphur recovery plants, one of which has been completed and the other of which is being built. They are both in the Alberta gas fields west of Windfall.
This trackage will consist of a branch line about 51 miles in length extending westerly from a point on the existing Canadian National line near Windfall to the Bigstone property of Pan American Petroleum Corporation, and also a spur about 9 miles long extending northerly from that line to the South Kaybob property of a syndicate headed by the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited. These properties represent important new industrial developments and new sources of sulphur and liquid petroleum gas and can be looked to for a substantial contribution to the economic activity of the region where they are located as well as to Canada's export trade.
The plant a Bigstone is already in production and the one at South Kaybob is well advanced with completion scheduled for November, 1968. The need for the service which the new rail facilities will provide is therefore pressing.
The estimated cost of the railway trackage including a crossing of the Athabasca river is $10,435,000, averaging approximately $174,000 per mile. In accordance with the usual practice the resolution authorizes the expenditure of that sum and allows for an additional 15 per cent if required to cover contingencies. The usual borrowing powers are also included.
The management of the C.N.R. has informed me that by means of traffic guarantee contracts made with the two companies whose names I have mentioned, the C.N.R. is assured that the products of these plants will be shipped over the new lines and over other lines of the C.N.R. in such volumes that the revenue therefrom will support all the costs of the lines and the movement of the traffic including amortization of the contemplated new capital investment and will also make a satisfactory contribution to the overhead of these railways, or that failing the shipment of such quantities of traffic compensatory payments will be made to the C.N.R. instead.
The new trackage will also stimulate industrial activity and the development of other resources in the area, including similar mineral prospects and the extensive timber resources in the Whitecourt forest district
October 1, 1968

through which the new lines will pass. Indeed, I can now state that a second sulphur plant at South Kaybob is already under construction and planned for completion late next year. There is also a strong likelihood that another such plant will shortly be developed along the route traversed by the new trackage.
Needless to say, any such activity so stimulated will not only benefit the business community generally but will also improve the contribution made to Canadian National's net return from these lines. I am, accordingly, satisfied that the economics and other justifications for the project contemplated by this resolution are sound, and I recommend this measure to the house.

The house resumed, from Monday, September 30, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Olson-Mr. Faulkner in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Farm Credit Act to broaden the classes of persons eligible for loans under the act; to increase the amount of the capital of the Farm Credit Corporation; to substitute for the present rates of interest on loans made under the act (except any such loans made pursuant to applications received by the corporation before September 13, 1968) such rate or rates of interest on any loans made after the coming into force of the said measure as may be prescribed by the governor in council; to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act and for other matters related or incidental thereto.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this resolution was last under discussion I was pointing out that there were really three forms of credit involved, only two of which are covered by the resolutions before us. The Farm Credit Corporation, of course, covers long term lending under a supervisory staff. The farmer puts a mortgage on his land and holdings as a guarantee for the loan.
The second type of credit available to the farmer is through the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This type of credit has been used principally, according to the reports made under that act, for the construction of buildings, the purchase of machinery and other basic improvements to the farm. This type of loan is generally secured, at least to some extent, by a chattel mortgage and is guaranteed by the government.
October 1, 1968

The third type of credit a farmer must use is similar to a business loan. This money is used to cover his operations, to purchase fertilizer, seed grain, gasoline for his tractor and other operating expenses, perhaps including food and the maintenance of his household. Such loans are granted on the basis of the credit rating the farmer has established with his entrepreneurs.
It is in this latter area, of course, that many farmers find the greatest difficulty and in which our legislation has not really been that all-embracing. However, it is in the first type of financing that I am most interested, that under the Farm Credit Corporation. This credit is the mainstay of the agricultural industry in Canada and it is in this area that the farmers' ability to make regular payments will be influenced by weather, crop conditions and so on.
In this field, Mr. Chairman, we learned a great deal from one particular man. I refer to the chairman under the Veterans Land Act, Mr. Rutherford, who passed away several years ago. Almost singlehanded, Mr. Rutherford looked at agricultural problems as they affected the war veterans who wished to go into agriculture. He was able to build the Veterans Land Act into an agency that covered the three types of financial requirements of the veterans going into agriculture. Most of these veterans were willing to accept supervision from the officials of that department who were highly qualified and always very sympathetic. Over the many years the Veterans Land Act was in operation, because of the co-operation of the department the losses amounted to less than 1 per cent. I feel that everyone would say, therefore, that it was a highly successful operation in the agricultural field and one which the Farm Credit Corporation tried to copy but without too much success.
First, in my opinion, the corporation failed to provide the type of supervisory staff necessary in this long term lending field. I know the chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation, and I know him to be a sincere, energetic civil servant working on behalf of the farmers of this country. However, the corporation has failed to convince the government that one of the ways a farmer has to be subsidized is in the obtaining of long range credit. The annual report of the Farm Credit Corporation for the year ended March 31, 1968 indicated that it had made loans to the tune of $263,236,500 and had lost $40,239. The total loss of the Farm Credit Corporation, including the
Farm Credit Act
operating loss, amounted to something like $3 million. I believe the minister will agree, because he has been on this side of the house and has certainly thought about the problem, that a $3 million loss covering the operating expenses is a very small price to pay for the support and expansion of agriculture in Canada. We are certainly subsidizing many other organizations that would not produce anywhere near the funds the Farm Credit Corporation has produced.
It is true that loans have been difficult to obtain. The report indicates that this year we are paying something over 6 per cent for money. I think the minister will agree, as a previous speaker pointed out, that the cost of borrowing money has fluctuated over the last 25 or 30 years from 3 per cent to 6 per cent. I am sure that if the minister reviews the 25-year period he will find great fluctuations in the prices farmers have received for their products. In general, however, those prices have not increased to an extent that would permit the farmer to pay double the interest rate he was paying. It seems to me, therefore, that either the farmer has to receive subsidies or the consumer will have to pay more for agricultural products. You can solve the problem one way or the other.
I am of the opinion that people in Canada are getting off very cheaply in so far as agricultural products are concerned. Let us use, as an example, the figures cited by the hon. member of the Ralliement Creditiste party who spoke yesterday. He mentioned that potatoes were selling at $1.50 per hundred pounds or 1J cents per pound. Anyone who knows anything about the production of potatoes will be aware that this price is well below the normal cost of production. A farmer would have to be in love with producing potatoes to produce them at that price. However, the consumer gets the benefit of low cost agricultural products in this field as well as others, including wheat products, dairy products and so on.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I am of the opinion that any increase in the mortgage rate is intolerable, and I would vote against any increase in the interest charged on Farm Credit Corporation loans. I would do so for a very simple reason. I would rather people did not enter the agricultural field today than see them spend the next ten years breaking their necks to repay a loan, probably ending up in the slum of some city because the corporation had taken over the farm. This sort of thing will happen as sure

October 1, 1968
Farm Credit Act
as I stand here. The farmer has no control over the marketing of his commodity or over the financing of his loan.
If governments in the past had not believed in subsidizing the farmers by fixing the interest rate over a 20 or 25-year period, then we would have left the matter to banks and other lending institutions in the mortgage field. If a farmer goes to his local credit union, caisse populaire or trust company and borrows money to buy gas for his truck or for his year's crop at 10 or 12 per cent and then goes bankrupt, the lending company, having charged him a high enough rate of interest in the first place, can afford to take its share of the loss. But when mortgages are granted to farmers I think the government has the responsibility of maintaining a reasonable rate of interest, and I consider 5 per cent to be reasonable.
I do not like wheat pools, Mr. Chairman, because although they are co-operatives they have tended to become so large that the membership has no say in their day to day operation, and in my opinion has not had too much say in some of the decisions that have been taken. However, in the publication, the Western Producer, the following appeared on the subject of farm credit:
Low returns to agriculture production often make interest rates higher than 5 per cent an excessive burden which hinders progress in agriculture in both the farmers' interests and the public's interest. It is therefore essential that through the Farm Credit Corporation or through an expanded and restructed federal agricultural credit service, a supervised "package" credit service be developed that can meet the short, intermediate and long term credit needs of farmers on a planned basis and at a moderate (i.e. 5 per cent) rate of interest. Such a service should very soon be made available.
I agree entirely with that comment. I believe that if the governor in council is allowed to set the rate of interest it will reach a similar level to that charged by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It will probably toe 1 percentage point higher than the current government rate at the time, and the rate for farmers will be in the range of 7 to 7J per cent on a long term mortgage. I ask, Mr. Chairman, what happens in the case of a calamity occurring, such as a crop failure? How long can you compound 6, 7 or 8 per cent interest? Any farmer will be able to provide the answer.
Therefore, it falls upon the minister to decide whether or not he should maintain the rate of interest on such loans at 5 per cent, this figure having been fairly representative of interest requirements in the market for the

last 30 years. If he does so, then the rate will have to be subsidized, but a $3 million subsidy on the part of the government on borrowings of $263 million does not seem to me unreasonable. Are we to charge an interest rate that will bankrupt the farmer, or oppose a bill that will give the farmer an inadequate money supply for expansion in the agricultural community? Personally, I would rather small farmers were not able to borrow money than see them charged a rate of interest at which they cannot repay their loans.
We have all seen those advertisements on television

I have taken part in some myself-where a man goes down to his local credit union, or whatever it is, and borrows money wisely, and all that sort of thing. However, I also know that this money has to be paid back. A worker who loses his job or gets sick for two or three weeks finds Household Finance sitting on his doorstep. I remember once working in an industry that went on strike, and I not only found the finance company on my doorstep but during the course of travelling around the country I found their agents in the lobby of every hotel at which I stayed. Certainly I would not want this sort of thing to happen to our farmers.
So far as the Farm Improvement Loans Act is concerned, I think that here the government is paying off an election debt. The government received a great deal of assistance during the last election campaign from finance and insurance companies. In my area some insurance companies had two or three people working in the election campaign, presumably because of some of the things I have said over a period of time about certain insurance companies. However, I am sure this sort of thing was general; I have heard it took place in a number of ridings.
If this legislation passes, certain finance, trust and insurance companies are going to set up an advisory body which will tell the farmers how to handle the money they lend them and help them in general. These companies do not need to help the farmers. The government is going to guarantee these loans. These loans will not be subject to an interest rate of 5 per cent; this has already been decided. Once the ceiling on interest rates has been lifted, these companies will be hungry for the market. And why not? This is a market in which the loans are guaranteed by the government, and so these companies cannot possibly lose.
I am aware of the fact that during the last 11 years many farmers have had difficulty borrowing money from banks and obtaining
October 1, 1968

credit. I am sure the minister also is well aware of this. Both of us have been here long enough to have participated many times in debates on the problems of the old legislation which set up the Canadian farm loans board. There was a total lack of respect in the agricultural community for that agency.
The minister and I also participated in the setting up of the Farm Credit Corporation, and I think that he will be the first to agree that this legislation, so far as the opposition was concerned, was patterned on the Veterans Land Act. We wrote into the legislation the supervised credit provisions contained in that act. As Canadians, I think we were proud of what we did under the Veterans Land Act, and to my mind one of our greatest accomplishments was the stabilization of the interest rate veterans had to pay over the years.
Similar provisions were put into the farming legislation because there was no one on either side of the house who did not agree that the agricultural community was experiencing difficulties in most of its operations. Farmers could not be saddled with a high interest rate when their returns produced an annual net income of something less than $3,000. Therefore, I hope that the minister will at least consider the provision of long term mortgages, as is the case under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and subsidize those loans so as to maintain the interest rate at 5 per cent. This is a field where we have to rely on private enterprise to put up the money, though, of course, we are furnishing guarantees.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I trust the minister will give serious consideration to retaining the present interest rate. Apart from anything else, this would serve as a yardstick by which the minister could measure the extent of treasury commitments by way of guarantee. I am sure the minister will bear this in mind, because he is as interested in the welfare of the agricultural community as I am, and no one believes he wants to return to the old days when people could lose their homes and property as a result of inability to pay excessive interest rates. I believe that the government, through subsidization, should over the long term bring about equality in interest rates levied on the mortgage type loans which are the backbone of financing in the agricultural community today.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on these three resolutions my opening remarks must be directed to the question of urgency to which the minister has referred. I
Farm Credit Act
wish to make it clear to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the country at large that it is parliament's duty to examine legislative proposals and the government's duty to regulate the order of business.
We were told that the measure which came up for discussion earlier today was urgently needed and that action should be taken in a hurry. We have been told that the farm improvement legislation has expired and that all the money available has been lent. It was the duty of the government to have called parliament one month earlier than it did so that all these matters could have been dealt with. If hon. gentlemen opposite continue to follow their present course they will wait until everything becomes urgent. Then we, as law-abiding members of the opposition, would be asked to forgo any opportunity to speak or to call attention to defects in the legislation, in favour of passing everything in a hurry. I wish to make it vividly clear why the government did not get unanimous consent to proceed to second reading of the previous bill.
The purpose of the farm improvement legislation a few years ago was to guarantee loans made by the banks so they could lend money to farmers. This act died on June 3, 1968 and it is now being reinstated to 1971. Three changes are proposed by the minister- a new interest rate, loans on land and an increase in the total amount of the permitted loans.
It is interesting to note that the minister's first piece of work for the Liberal government in parliament is to introduce three bills each of which contains provisions for increased interest rates. Consider this in the light of the minister's background. For years and years he campaigned in Alberta in favour of lower interest rates, particularly for the agricultural industry. Yet the first stroke of business he does after crossing the fence is to present parliament with three bills each of which increases interest rates. I wonder what his friends back home will think of this stroke of business. I am certain that the farmers do not consider higher interest rates a necessity today though it may well be that the government does. Remember, it was a Liberal government which two years ago took the ceiling off interest rates, and we all saw what happened last year. They shot skyward. Fortunately, they are now receding somewhat, but this government is still not happy. They want carte blanche to allow them to increase interest rates at any time in connection with this piece of farm legislation.

October 1, 1968
Farm Credit Act
In this context it is interesting to recall what the minister himself said about farm income, upon which rests the ability to repay these loans. It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to say that this bill will increase the amount available to farmers from $15,000 to $25,000. It is not the government which will lend this money. The banks will be asked to lend it and the banks will not lend it unless the borrowers can repay these amounts. That is the sole criterion.
In an article on agricultural policy which appeared in the Leader-Post on July 27, 1968, the minister is quoted as saying:
The mechanics of the solutions may be different, but getting costs and receipts far enough apart so there is a reasonable income left is what is needed.
I ask the minister my first question. Are these proposals likely to get costs and receipts far enough apart so there is a reasonable income left? The answer is obvious. They are not. How can they when the hon. gentleman has increased one of the farmer's basic costs?
We on this side of the house recall some of the remarks made by the minister in the course of a previous debate on this subject in April, 1966, as reported in Hansard at page 4325. This is what he told us with regard to increasing the money available to farmers:
Finally, I want to say that there has been an alarming increase in the price of farm machinery. We had a manifestation of the concern in this regard yesterday in the house. I am wondering whether there has not been an increase in the price of farm machinery because the maximum amount available to an individual farmer was raised from $7,500 to $15,000 only a short time ago.
While I do not accept his premise, I ask the minister a second question: Is it logical, then, to expect that if the permitted amount of loan is increased from $15,000 to $25,000 the price of farm machinery will go up? When we sat on the agricultural committee and studied this question the machine manufacturers bare facedly admitted that they charged what the market would bear. It was as clear as that. Now the minister proposes giving the farmers more money. Is it logical to suppose that the machine companies, for a time at any rate, will try to capitalize on the situation, at least until they realize that in a few years the farmers will be broke?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES. ETC.
speechtext: Has the hon. member read the statement that I made last night?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES. ETC.
speechtext:
I read the whole speech and I found it most unenlightening. It contained a number of hidden suggestions and I propose

to deal with them quickly. The minister talked about bigger guaranteed loans to farmers and said the size of the average loan to farmers had increased. I am concerned about the ability of the industry to pay back these loans.
What do we see happening? One of the three agencies of the wheat board, James Richardson and Sons, states that it has never seen the wheat marketing position look so poor as it does today. What does the government say? I saw the minister of industry on television the other day and he said: "Well, we cannot say; we have big hopes; we shall make a statement in a day or two." Mr. Chairman, all of western Canada is in a state of uncertainty.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We have had a difficult fall. I believe the farmers will get their crops off the land, but they want to know whether the government is making a firm attempt to market their wheat. Here is an article I clipped from the Manitoba Co-Operator. The heading reads, "Canadian Action Hurts Wheat Sales." Is that a very encouraging heading? The article dealt with the Canberra meeting and said in part that of the five major exporting nations that met at Canberra the United States was the only one complaining. It complained about Australia's pricing policies and about France's pricing policies. Canada, the article said, was not complaining. Canada was in a conciliatory mood and was prepared to work things out.
Does this give encouragement to our farmers and help them to put up with the troubles that nature has provided them with this fall? It does not. It signifies to the farmers that the government does not care. The United States is fighting the battles of the Canadian wheat farmer. The United States set a target for its wheat exports of 750 million bushels last year, and this year it has announced the same target figure. What target have we had from our government?
As I said, the minister went on television and shrugged his shoulders. This shrugging of shoulders is becoming a very popular habit on television today. The minister said, "We cannot really say, but we have got a couple of good announcements to come." If there were good announcements to come a grain marketing firm like James Richardson would not have said that it never saw the market prospects look gloomier.
The minister's basic responsibility is to assure that the agricultural industry will be
October 1, 1968

able to pay back the loans that he is advocating through this and the other two resolutions. What about farm machinery sales during the past year? It is a well known fact that bankers will lend only that amount of money that a person is able to pay back. A person can increase his farm machinery requirements from $25,000 to $45,000 but the banks will not advance him the difference.
While I am dealing with the subject of bankers lending money I would point out that many hon. members have stood in this house and said that the agricultural industry is a good credit industry, and that only one-tenth of one per cent of the amount of loans made by the Farm Credit Corporation were not repaid. However, banks do not have a good reputation with regard to taking risks. This farm improvement loans legislation guarantees up to 10 per cent of an individual bank's losses. Why have the banks not taken a greater risk? Why have they not been prepared to take a greater risk? I suppose the reason is that they would say: We are not too confident of the agricultural industry in Canada.
We have not seen the government nail down an agricultural policy. When the former minister of agriculture was asked a question about agricultural policy he replied "I have set up an advisory policy group in that regard and they are going to bring down a policy pretty soon." The present minister said the same thing last night-"Wait until I hear from my policy advisers." They are four university professors. If they ever got into a barnyard they would not know their way out of it. What kind of policy will they produce?
Machinery manufacturers charge all the market will bear. I point out that machine sales this year are down drastically-34 per cent in the province of Saskatchewan, 22 per cent in Manitoba, and 26.6 per cent in the province of Alberta. According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, these three provinces purchase over 60 per cent of all the farm machinery bought in Canada. This gives some idea of the present state of confidence in the agricultural industry. Farm machinery sales would not be down if farmers and bankers had confidence in the industry. Yet the government is reluctant to make a forecast of market prospects for wheat this year.
It is a well known fact, based on Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures, that farm net income corresponds directly to the amount of wheat sales. I would like to quote from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics annual report on farm net income, in the hope of showing 29180-421
Farm Credit Act
the great need for the minister to come out and state emphatically what his policies and objectives are. The report states:
Total farm net income... which takes into account changes in farm inventories of field crops and livestock, amounted to $1,529.1 million in 1967, 21.2 per cent below the 1966 record-
This gives some idea of the problem confronting the industry today. What are the prospects with regard to 1968 farm net income? I was going to say that wheat sales are down something like 50 per cent but the figure is not quite that. They are down a good 33 per cent. Total wheat sales, including flour, for the crop year ended 1968 were down $330 million. Yet we hear the Minister of Agriculture say, "You cannot have a subsidized interest rate because it gets things out of whack in the economy and the economists advise against it."
But the government has no trouble guaranteeing the automobile manufacturers a subsidy of $50 million a year. It has no trouble guaranteeing subsidies to other sectors of the economy. However, when the agricultural industry asks that its interest rate not be increased the minister suggests that he cannot do anything about it. He was the one who cried for years in the province of Alberta that interest rates were too high. We now find him advocating that they should be higher.
I should now like to direct my remarks to the Farm Credit Corporation. The Farm Credit Corporation was devised out of the old farm loan board. It was specifically designed to help farmers who could not definitely be stated to have efficient units. But in the past few years we have seen a drift in the direction of the Farm Credit Corporation helping farmers who are on what might be called efficient and economic units.
It is high time that the whole question of the Farm Credit Corporation and its policies be referred to the standing committee on agriculture. As I read the minister's remarks last night he talked about the advisability of making Farm Credit Corporation loans available to Indians and other people. The resolution is very specific in that regard. It speaks of:
-a measure to amend the Farm Credit Act to broaden the classes of persons eligible for loans under the act;
That is a broad statement. I believe that the whole question of the Farm Credit Corporation's policies should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture which could deal with all aspects.

October 1, 1968
Farm Credit Act
As recorded on page 4324 of Hansard for April 26, 1966, the Minister of Agriculture said:
If we refer to the records of the Farm Credit Corporation we find that the regulations applicable to young people have perhaps been a little too rigid.
Last night he said that he agreed that regulations have to be made under which a father and son can carry on a business in co-operation with one another. Has this not been the policy? If it has been, why is it not working? Certainly it was our understanding of the Farm Credit Corporation legislation that farms could be passed from father to son without too much difficulty.
I think everyone on this side of the chamber, including members to my left and right if they come from agricultural areas, is well aware of the fact that the Farm Credit Corporation has done a tremendous job. But I know that the minister, if he were not occupying a seat in the cabinet, would be the first to agree with me that during the last few years there has been a tendency for the Farm Credit Corporation to slip away from its original purposes and intent.
I am quite prepared to let the farm improvement loans legislation go through as rapidly as possible, but I say without any hesitation that the Farm Credit Corporation legislation and the policies of the corporation should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture. Not since its inception in 1959 has the Farm Credit Corporation been examined by the agricultural committee in any real sense.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I remember well when the farm machinery syndicate bill was before parliament. At that tune the minister said that this matter could be taken back to the agricultural committee every year if we did not like it. He said that it could be referred to the committee and reviewed by the members of the committee every year. Since it was passed I have noticed that the regulations have been changed and that loans are now being made on buildings. Under the original bill each farmer had to sign a guarantee covering the total amount of his loan. In the proposed resolution we see that the corporations, co-operatives and so on will all be eligible and that individual members will not be broken down. I take it that if a corporation is formed in such a manner that each farmer is responsible only for his share of the net borrowings of the corporation the

corporation still will qualify for a farm syndicate loan.
Under the old bill, if seven farmers could join together to borrow $100,000 I did not see any sense in each one of those seven farmers having to guarantee the $100,000. This is the way the original bill was drawn up. I believe that each farmer should guarantee only that portion for which he is responsible and not the total amount. I certainly would like to think that this could be dealt with having in mind the reason the farm syndicate legislation has not been the success the minister concerned thought it would be. I believe the number of loans has been approximately 444. The minister can correct me if I am wrong. Therefore it has not been the success the minister thought it would be. Why has it not been a success? It has done a good job with regard to the lending of money to families but it really has not broadened its scope. Loans to farmers for building purposes would aid the farmers generally.
We on this side of the house believe the interest rate on Farm Credit Corporation loans should not be allowed to increase. There is nothing wrong with the subsidization of loans for a period in respect of the agricultural industry when that industry is in difficulty as it certainly is today. When I first became a member of parliament many years ago the Farm Loan Board was making a profit and paying income tax on that profit. If the minister doubts my words he can look at the records for the year 1956-57. This is an indication that interest rates can fluctuate over the years. The corporation can make loans for a period of up to 30 years. In that period, 5 per cent might balance out to be exactly the right rate or perhaps even too much. Certainly it is not necessary to have a fluctuating rate. This would mean, for instance, that when the agricultural industry is in difficulty the interest rate would be high and when the agricultural industry is operating on a sound basis the interest rate would be lower. The opposite should be true. When the industry is in trouble the government should lower the interest rate and when the industry is buoyant perhaps it no longer requires subsidization.
I doubt that the minister would say that he is increasing the interest rate today because the agricultural industry is backward. Perhaps we should take a look at the situation round the world today. In the United States the question being asked is whether they should pay the farmer more than $10,000 a year not to farm. The dairy industry in the
October 1, 1968

United States is subsidized to the hilt. One might look at the situation in respect of the European common market. Wheat and almost every other agricultural product are subsidized. Pork is subsidized to the amount of approximately $14 a hundredweight. In the Netherlands, for example, a pound of Cheddar cheese worth 55 cents is selling for 17 cents a pound. In other words, they are subsidizing their dairy industry.
There is no question in my mind about the fact that the agricultural industry is today one of the basic industries of this country. It is one of the main employers of this country, perhaps even a greater employer than the federal government and all other governments combined. To the surprise of many people in the province of Alberta the agricultural industry there is still the main employer. What is this government doing? It is not allowing the net income of the farmer to increase. Rather, it is allowing his costs to increase and thereby accentuating the cost-prize squeeze. The government very recently increased the farmer's costs by allowing the St. Lawrence seaway charges to increase another percentage point.
We are told that the government does not know what the wheat sales will be this year. We are told that there are great expectations for the next three years averaged together, but we do not know about this year. Sales are necessary now when the agricultural industry finds itself in a state of flux. Grain sales are off, farm net income is low and more people are leaving the farms. They are not necessarily leaving because they want to but because their income is not comparable with that of those in other parts of our society.
It is the duty of the minister to ensure that all those who are engaged in the farming industry today earn an income comparable with that earned in other sectors of our society so that they will be in a position to pay back the amount of money he is prepared to lend them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, several hon. members have indicated already that the Minister of Agriculture, in effect, is guaranteeing a sound and sure thing to the financial institutions. As a farmer, a backbencher and a new member I had the impression that the Minister of Agriculture had the responsibility of looking after the interests of the farmers. Perhaps I am mistaken. In view of some of the speeches which have been made some doubt has been
Farm Credit Act
raised in my mind. As a farmer and a member representing an agricultural district I feel a certain measure of insecurity and doubt about the position of the agricultural industry in western Canada. This is the only industry about which I can speak with any authority.
There has been considerable doubt in my mind about the policies of the present Minister of Agriculture and the desire of the government to do something about solving the farmers' problems. One thing I am sure of; I am aware of how much money I am not making. We have had this experience before in the field of agriculture. If the Minister of Agriculture is a farmer he must have had a certain amount of experience of this kind. We are guaranteeing to the financial institutions a sure thing in the lending of this money to farmers. Are the farmers to be the ones to take the risk and to become the entrepreneurs of the new society? Are they to take the risk while the financial institutions are given a higher rate of interest? I understand the interest rate has gone up because the risk has increased. I assume that the Minister of Agriculture is a farmer and that he is interested in the problems of the farmer. I assume also that he is determined to proceed with the legislation which is on the order paper. Therefore I wish to make some suggestions to him in respect of some items which I think might improve the legislation.
First, I should like to suggest that any lending institution that is not familiar with the farming industry should not be allowed to lend money under this legislation. Farmers can get into enough trouble without advice from those who have no particular interest in the industry except to make money.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that interest payments should not have to be made more than once a year. Frequently when you borrow money from a bank you are required to pay interest once a month or at least once every six months. This is a compounding of interest rates and in direct conflict with the Farm Improvement Loans Act as it has been. Under that act interest payment has only been required once a year.
It is my belief that the interest rate should be set by parliament. If we cannot set an absolute rate here, we should have a formula whereby it is tied to the bank rate and it should not be higher than 1 per cent above that bank rate. I have the uneasy feeling that if we allow rates to be set by order in council they will be higher than we are now paying.

October 1, 1968
Farm Credit Act
If a bank or lending institution is to receive a guarantee from the government the interest rate should not be too high.
Let me turn for a moment to the Farm Credit Act. I asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture last evening about broadening the classes of individuals under the act. As yet I have received no reply. It is my suggestion that under this act only practising farmers should receive loans. I am not opposed to government boards or agencies lending money to anyone else, but that should be done under some other act or authority. Let us restrict eligibility under this act to practising farmers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES. ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member whether he is referring to the F.C.C. when he makes that statement?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES. ETC.
speechtext:
I was
referring to the Farm Credit Corporation, yes. Eligibility should only pertain to practising farmers. I want to refer particularly to those people I feel the Farm Credit Corporation should be considering. If there is to be a broadening of the classes of individuals eligible for loans, I suggest the loans should be made to those who need them most. The terms under which those who wish to borrow money can qualify should be broadened.
It may be that loans should only be made on the basis of an individual's ability to farm, but that is not the case at this time. One has to have a certain equity, and if you do not have a rich family or a well known friend you will never get a loan. It does not matter how efficient a farmer you may be or how shrewd a businessman you are, you require a certain amount of money. I hope the minister will consider broadening the aspects of the act in this regard.
Let me tell you about a young farmer with whom I was discussing the problem of getting started in farming. I asked why the Farm Credit Corporation could not buy economic units as such and lease them to young farmers with suitable qualifications for a period of five or ten years. At a later date they could have an option to purchase the farm. This young farmer, who was not of the same political persuasion as myself, agreed with me and suggested that if the Farm Credit Corporation purchased economic units they should be leased only to young farmers who wished to start farming.
In my district many farmers are reaching the age when they will wish to dispose of their farm units. Many of them have built up

reasonably successful and fairly large units. There is a shortage of young farmers who are in a position to get started, and I think it only reasonable that we provide a more effective way of acquiring farm units for those who wish to farm and do not have adequate backing. Very often a father who is able to start his son in farming finds that his son does not wish to stay at home. Often it is necessary for a farmer with four or five sons to obtain assistance to get them established.
I repeat that we in parliament should set the interest rate. This is government money we are discussing and we should have some control in this regard. If the Minister of Agriculture becomes ashamed of what the interest rate is I think he should let us know. If he is not prepared to allow parliament to set the interest rate I feel the bill should be referred to the committee on agriculture where it can be thoroughly discussed.
Under the provisions of these two acts I think it will be possible for farmers to borrow enough money to get started, purchase machinery and operate efficient economic units, as we understand them in west central Saskatchewan where there are many such units. With higher interest rates costs will increase and it will be very difficult even for those who have large economic units to make any money. I discussed this matter with a farm loans manager who said it was becoming more difficult for the individual farmer to obtain an adequate net return, in spite of the fact he may have $100,000 or $150,000 tied up in his particular enterprise. This is the opinion of a man who should know, and he had no axe to grind with me. We were just discussing this matter in a practical way.
What will happen to those farmers or operators who for reasons beyond their control find themselves without enough money to continue operations? Obviously the minister has recognized agriculture as a commercial industry rather than as a subsistence activity. I suggest to him that it is not enough to settle for adequate capital and encouragement to individual farmers to take courses in farm management. We must also have volume of production at adequate prices. I am sure that the minister, who is the operator of a fairly large farm, I understand, realizes the importance of volume and what happens when volume decreases. If we do not sell a great deal of our farm production we will soon see a lot of individual farmers in trouble. This is not only true of farmers but also of those who service their industry such as farm dealers and others. They too depend on large volume
October 1. 1968

businesses, and a very small margin off the top can put them in trouble.
The situation in respect of the sale of grain has been discussed in this house during the debate on the throne speech and at other times. Apparently the Minister of Agriculture cannot or will not do anything about grain sales. He refers the matter to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He does not know what to do about the situation so he refers it to the Prime Minister. Obviously the Prime Minister, with no farming background, does not know what to do about it so he discusses it with the flower children. Where does this leave the farmer? It is high time something was done.
With all due respect to the Minister of Agriculture, let us not separate capital requirements and farm management from the marketplace and prices that are adequate if the farmer is to make a going thing of his particular economic enterprise.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the
representative of a riding where 35 per cent of the people are farmers, I would like to say a few words about the resolution of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) to extend the definition of the categories of people who can get loans, to increase the capital of the Farm Credit Corporation, etc.
I am a little worried about that possibility of allowing people other than bona fide farmers to secure those loans, because the day might come when someone will buy so much land that he will be able to control what we call a parish in Quebec. That worries me in the sense that there would then be a controller of farm life who would not be interested in keeping up the operation of that family farm in Quebec which, although larger today, must not be abandoned.
I have often heard-and I was able to check that information-that, in Quebec and even throughout Canada, for every 30 farms whose operation is abandoned a hospital must be built. Many hospitals are now built because seeds do not contain, through good family farming-the vitamins or fertilizers necessary to their growth. Those products are not wholesome for Canadians as they used to be.
Farming has been commercialized and I see in this resolution the possibility that some businessmen may take advantage of the borrowing right and end up by controlling
Farm Credit Act
unduly large farms. If there is unemployment now in Canada, why should we stop operating family farms which enabled father, mother and children to work together, especially if we consider the farming vocation of the province of Quebec, and let one single man control a whole parish, as I was saying earlier.
I am in favour of the family farm so that farm products which used to be healthful for our people may continue to be so. Indeed, our farmers of the province of Quebec, thanks to the family farm which they had operated well, had succeeded in maintaining the health of our Canadian citizens.
A review of the figures quoted by the Minister of Agriculture shows a number of astronomical loans, that is 72,000 loans for a total of $1,100 million.
Taking those figures into account, I would like to know how many Quebecers have taken advantage of this legislation? It is probably one of the reasons which explains the massive desertion of farms in Quebec, because the loans were never granted in that province in the same way as in the rest of Canada.
I do not object to the prosperity of agriculture in the west or in other parts of Canada. But I also wish that agriculture in Quebec would be profitable, because at the present time, a considerable number of farmers apply for social welfare, because the family farm does not provide them with a living.
In 1962, when the minister sat on this side of the house, I had asked-he is aware of it, and this could be done this year also, since we can now buy feed grains at a low cost and without delay-that grain elevators be built which would allow the eastern farmers to purchase feed grains at a lower cost.
I am not sure, but it seems to me there should be limits to borrowing, to giving more rope for anyone to strangle himself even more. Let us permit the farmer to manage his farm and earn sufficient income to live decently.
If we allow the farmers to borrow even more money at higher interest rates, this will certainly play us a nasty trick, as was the case when banks were allowed to lend money at higher interest rates; we see today that the financial sharks, the bankers are eating each other up. Tomorrow, farmers will be chased after in an effort to lend them money, and little by little they will be strangled, because agriculture does not pay.
A while ago someone said, and I read it in the papers, that an additional subsidy of two

October 1, 1968
Farm Credit Act
cents per pound would be paid tor butter. But, and this came right after, that subsidy would be used to pay for its storage. The farmer then will not feel any of its effects. We would need immediate measures.
The other day I heard the hon. Minister of Trade, Commerce and Industry (Mr. Pepin) say in the house that the western wheat posed problems. I know, even now, a company in Quebec, which is ready to supply us with a barge to go and get the grain out west, to transport it down the St. Lawrence seaway, unload it at a seaport, so that the farmers can go and get it. They would then have some income to enable the family farm to keep on progressing.
Grains keep much longer in elevators, but even during the fall, with the nice weather we are having in Quebec, if the barge were loaded over there and came to the eastern ports the farmers could organize a bee and purchase wheat at $1 or $1.50 less per hundredweight. Then the undertaking would be profitable. We do not ask for permission to choke the farmer a little more. What we ask, is the right for him to a better income. This would be much better than making loans of $50,000 or $60,000 available. One always says, and there is a truth therein: "Tell me who is helping you financially and I will tell you who is taking advantage of you."
You want to broaden the provisions of the Farm Credit Act. This is only logical and I do not see any objection to it. What I object to is that we would do this to the prejudice of the family farm in Quebec. Why do we not take example on the Quebec agricultural legislation which provides for the repayment of the interest rate on loans. It seems to me we could provide for a rebate of this kind on federal farm loans. This would help directly the farmer who is even now leaving the farm to join the crowd of people depending on social security cheques for their living.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Social welfare for these people now amounts to $248 millions. Whether we want to or not, we have to grant social welfare and build hospitals. That money is spent nevertheless although there is no help for the farmers.
Therefore, as representatives of the province of Quebec and in the case of my constituency where 35 per cent of the population are farmers, we ask for the immediate adoption of legislation that will contribute towards

the true restoration of the family farm. Considering the figures I have just given, I maintain that, at the present time, Quebec is not benefitting from loans as its agriculture is not profitable anymore. Produce is being imported from the United States through commercially organized farms where the land is over-cultivated. It must be remembered that over-cultivated land will, in the end, not yield what the country needs as a minimum for feeding its people.
I would myself ask another question. If the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Cote) has a word to say about the farmers, why does he not contribute something that would be really helpful to the province of Quebec? Perhaps the parliamentary secretary has forgotten that his party had promised the appointment of a Minister of Agriculture for Eastern Canada. That promise never materialized and it melted with the spring snow. That had been promised in January and its realization would have assisted the eastern farmers as distinctions could have been made between problems of western and eastern Canada so that solutions could have been found.
These problems, however, are not yet settled. Feed grain is sold at prices which simply exploit the farmer, for government subsidies for transportation by rail are given to the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. instead of being given to the farmers. In my riding, the feed grain could be moved by truck and delivered to the farmers, which would allow them to make more money. I would like to see credit given for initiatives like these, instead of the money going to people who will commercialize the farms, for there has been too much of that in the past. We must go back to what we have known in Quebec, and that is why we ask the Minister of Agriculture to take concrete steps.
Since I came to this house, on September 12, or since my election on June 25, I have concerned myself with this problem of feed grain in the hope of increasing the farmer's income and of stopping the commercialization of family farms. A company agreed to provide a barge which would fetch feed grain free of charge; that would mean a higher income for the farmer. We would then see fewer of these $25,000 or $30,000 loans at interest rates which are too high and which prevent our farmers from having an income which would allow them to live decently.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I ask the minister not to make it too easy to borrow at any
October 1, 1968

price, for we have had one bad experience of this sort with the banks when we allowed them to lend money at uncontrolled interest rates. Everyone regrets this step which was taken, but it is too late, for the legislation has been passed. I therefore ask the minister to consider all aspects of the situation, so that we will not have to go back on our decision later.
