speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to speak on the three resolutions before us because I was a member of the agricultural committee at the time the Farm Credit Act was first brought in and I recall much of the action that took place. There was a great need for such a bill. However, I am certainly in wholehearted agreement with what was said by the hon. member for Crowfoot this afternoon when he proposed that this resolution be placed before the standing committee on agriculture because it is my view that it is necessary to amend and review this legislation from time to time.
As will be recalled, when the Farm Credit Act was first brought in its primary purpose was to help young farmers to get a start because we found in western Canada that young people were increasingly being forced away from farms and consequently farms were being deserted and left to elderly people who had to try to carry on by themselves. The introduction of the act brought a ray of hope to farmers in western Canada because it gave an opportunity to young people to obtain capital to work on farms and enabled the senior citizens to retire.
I found that as time went on we drifted away from the goals which we set for ourselves under this legislation, and it is now helping to a larger extent the big farmers. I have noticed that in recent years many young people must be subsidized in order to stay on their farms but their applications for loans have been turned down and they have had to take on other employment so as to enable them to continue farming. The farming situation in Canada has worsened to the point where farmers must be subsidized in this day and age. Farming is the life of these people and what they want to do, but in many cases they can only be part time farmers and must take other employment in order to meet their obligations and to put their farms on a sound economic footing.
I therefore support the proposal made by the hon. member for Crowfoot that before
Farm Credit Act
this resolution is passed by the house it should be considered in the agricultural committee. I strongly urge the government to refer this resolution to the committee before it makes any changes in the Farm Credit Corporation.
We realize the value of farm improvement loans. Farmers must have this credit in order to carry on. There is no point in having farm improvement loan legislation if there is no money available because the rate of interest is too low and banks do not want to lend money. This is what we have experienced in the past years. I do not think there would be any harm in having this matter discussed in the agricultural committee.
I think consideration must be given to increasing the amount of capital of the Farm Credit Corporation because farmers have had to increase the size of their farms. At present this is an economic necessity. Farmers must have sufficient capital to purchase the necessary machinery and farms must be large enough to be economic. This amendment to the act is very necessary.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I should like to point out that there are many farmers on smaller units. These people must crawl before they can walk. I have known qualified farmers, men who have been raised on the farm and decided to make farming their life work, who have been turned down when they applied for loans. As I pointed out, I for one feel that I would not like to see the interest rate on Farm Credit Corporation loans allowed to fluctuate at will because I feel this would be very detrimental.
I feel differently about the other resolution covering farm improvement loans. As I pointed out, we saw what happened last summer when there was no money available to make farm improvement loans. We saw what happened to business throughout western Canada. The lack of business was noticeable because people were unable to purchase much needed machinery when farm improvement loans were not available.
I do not intend to dwell very long on the third resolution concerning the co-operative purchase of farm machinery. I have been unable to find that this idea has worked to the advantage of the farmers. There are certain types of machinery that farmers can own jointly. In my part of the country, however, farmers have to do their work in seasonable weather, so it is not too long until

October 1, 1968
Farm Credit Act
they want to own their machinery. I do not believe this act has been used to any extent in my district. Years ago there were machinery syndicates, but I have been unable to find any such syndicates in my district today except where a family is concerned.
I urge upon the minister that before any great changes are made in the Farm Credit Corporation the matter should be brought before the committee on agriculture. In so far as farm improvement loans are concerned, as I have said there is no point in having the legislation on the books if the interest rate is such that there is no money to borrow.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in the debate on this resolution, I first of all want to comment upon the minister's reference to the urgency of expediting the passage of this measure. I can certainly sympathize with this attitude, and I do not want to see the mounting pile of letters on his desk get any higher before some action is taken. Nevertheless, I trust he will try to forgive me if I suggest that there is a very heavy responsibility on the Liberal party for the delay in introducing legislation on this subject. I trust the minister is not suggesting the corollary of this particular statement because I feel that proper discussion of this legislation is required. I suggest that adequate discussion of this measure should in no way be considered as delaying its passage or implementation. It seems to me there are some fundamental points we do need to consider in dealing with this resolution.
First of all, I think that farm credit cannot be considered in isolation from general farm policies and programs. I think that credit can be a trap if it is not tied in with other farm programs to ensure that every farmer will have adequate returns for his produce. In this regard I noted this statement the minister made as recorded in Hansard for yesterday, page 599:
The objectives of the program are to provide the capital to facilitate the organization of Canadian agriculture into viable farm units in the hands of our competent farmers so that agriculture may make the greatest possible contribution to the Canadian economy and provide farmers with equitable returns for their investment of capital, work and skills.
I agree that in so far as the provision of capital does assist in bringing about an efficient farm enterprise it does contribute to the farmer's well-being. Nevertheless, this is no substitute for adequate legislation to ensure that the farmer does have adequate

returns for the produce he takes to the market as a result of the capital investment he has made.
The second fundamental point that I think needs to be commented upon has already been dealt with by a number of hon. members. I do not intend to deal with it at any great length. Nevertheless, I have to refer to it. I refer to the lack of a comprehensive approach to the credit problem. I feel that we have in the proposals before us at the present time a patch-work program rather than an adequate, comprehensive approach to credit problems.
The third fundamental point, I think, is illustrated in the government proposal to allow interest rates to be set by market forces. I suggest that in fact this means throwing the farmers to the wolves because the farmer has to operate in an economy where he does not have adequate bargaining power, where he does not have economic power of the same degree and nature as that possessed by many other people in other sectors of the Canadian economy. At the present time in this country we have high interest rates. This is a fact in every sector of the economy. One example that has been referred to in this house in recent weeks has been the housing situation and the high interest rates connected with housing. The farmer is also going to have to accept his share of the bill to pay for the mess that has been created by this government.
I believe that the government has to take the responsibility for the skyrocketing interest rates in Canada today. This came about following the revision of some of our monetary legislation at the time the Bank Act was revised and some other measures were before the house. I was not here but it has been confirmed by other members that the present Minister of Agriculture voted against some of the revisions of the Bank Act and the change in the interest rate structure. The fact is that the problems of the farmers were known before 1963 and result, as I pointed out, from the low degree of bargaining power the agricultural industry has in our present economic structure. Given that situation, we may have to recognize that even though it may be wrong we are going to have to levy high interest rates. What dc we do, then, with regard to the agricultural industry, an industry that is in a very poor economic position within the total framework of the Canadian economy? There are several alternatives, and I think the government should consider some of them.
October 1, 1968

The first alternative is for the government to ensure that the farmer has adequate bargaining power through orderly marketing machinery and also, where necessary, guarantee a proper price for his produce. The second alternative is to hold down interest rates and, if necessary to accomplish this, provide the capital for our farm credit program. The third alternative is to subsidize interest rates where necessary. I suggest that these alternatives should be looked at by the government before this legislation is put in final form.
In taking a look at the proposed amendments to this act I note, of course, its extension to credit unions and caisse populaires. They can also lend money under the provisions of the Farm Credit Act. Yesterday the minister made a reference to the extension of the Farm Credit Corporation legislation to Indian reserves. All hon. members in the house applauded this proposal when the minister brought it before us. Certainly I feel that the idea is good, but when one takes a closer look at this provision I believe there are some serious questions that should be asked and answered. The minister stated yesterday, as recorded on page 600 of Hansard:
It would seem appropriate that the corporation be given authority to enter into appropriate agreements with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development so that appropriate arrangements can be made to provide credit for the development of viable farm businesses on Indian reserves.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This is fine in terms of fulfilling the objective of enabling the Indian people to develop farm enterprises on Indian reserve lands. However, I should also like to suggest that there are some fundamental questions here. The first of these is the fact that these agreements will have to be made with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I quite recognize, of course, that in framing any particular act the minister will have to live within the confines of the legislation now existing. However, I suggest for the consideration of all members that once again we are tying in here programs that are designed to help the Indian people with our present framework within which Indian people are completely dependent upon the benevolence of the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I think, we need to take a look at the principle involved. Certainly I should like to inquire of the minister whether in fact there were consultations with the Indian people
Farm Credit Act
prior to bringing this proposal forward. I hope this was the case. I also hope that as a result of any agreements arrived at the Indian people will be able to deal directly with the Farm Credit Corporation instead of having to go through the administrative framework of the Indian affairs branch. I am sure that the minister and many hon. members are aware of the serious delays that have been encountered by many Indian people who have attempted to do something to advance their own economic position.
I have one example before me, Mr. Chairman, of the type of intolerable delays that exist so far as the Indian people are concerned. I have before me a letter addressed to the director of Indian affairs in Ottawa. It is from Mr. Harry Buffalo who lives on the Moose Wood reserve which is south of Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Copies of the letter were sent to the hon. member for Moose Jaw and to a number of others as well. I should like to quote some parts of the letter in order to indicate the type of difficulty many Indian people experience in their relations with the Indian affairs branch. While I am not in a position specifically to confirm the contents of this letter, I can say from my own personal experience that I have run into similar cases of frustrating delay encountered by the Indian people. Mr. Harry Buffalo states:
During the last few years I have been trying to build up a cattle herd to become self-sufficient.
I now have 51 head of Hereford cattle, 10 of which I bought by a loan from the department of Indian affairs.
The problem is the lack of haying equipment. The Band obtained (this spring) new haying equipment complete with baler. This haying equipment has been used exclusively by the overseer and his family, these people have no more than ten head of cattle among them and the hay has been put up and sold privately, with the result I have no hay to winter my stock.
On August 2nd, 1968, I went to Regina and saw Mr. Reid. He suggested I see Mr. Hanson at the Duck Lake agency. Mr. Hanson was to send a man to Moose Wood reserve but he never came. (If he did he didn't come to see me.)
Mr. Reid said that I would need $450 as a down payment to buy equipment through the revolving fund. This presents no problem as I could sell two head of cattle to raise this amount or I could borrow this amount from the credit union if I had a statement from the Indian department that I am eligible for he revolving fund loan. (If and when I can get any action from the department of Indian affairs).
I have been to Duck Lake numerous times to see where I stand with getting the use of the hay equipment now on the reserve. My last effort was three weeks ago when I had a lawyer contact Mr. Ivan Ahenkew at Duck Lake. Mr. Ahenkew said he would be down to see me the following Monday, but never came. (He came to the reserve

October 1, 1968
Farm Credit Act
about a week ago and came to the house, but did not bother to come where I work or wait for me.)
I hope you can picture the position I am in:
1.	The haying equipment which is now on the reserve has not been made available to me and I want to know why this equipment has been used only by the overseer Mr. Wm. Eagle and his family.
2.	The delays in Regina for not going ahead as promised so I could buy my own equipment.
3.	The promises from Mr. Ivan Ahenkew and others at Duck Lake to get in touch with me and straighten these matters out. Promises that were never kept.
We have heard a lot recently about making the Indian self-sufficient. My family are all getting good educations and I am trying to bring them up as good Canadians but how can anyone get ahead getting the run around from supervisors, regional director's office in Regina, Indian agents and other buck passers whose word and promises are no good ...
It is too late now to save all of my breeding stock, some will have to be sold to winter the rest.
Please see that I am not in this same position next year, anything your department can do at your level would certainly be appreciated.
Yours very truly,
Harry Buffalo
This, Mr. Chairman, is the type of situation that I know has been experienced time and time again by Indian people in dealing with the Indian affairs branch.
One of the resolutions before us amends the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act, and some references have already been made to this act. I think there is no question that if we are going to amend the Farm Credit Act, this act should also be amended so as to maintain consistency in the legislation. I certainly approve and go along with the proposed extension to co-operative associations.
A question has been asked by some people that I should like to hear the minister answer. Who is using the act? It has been suggested that it is mainly the large farmers who are already quite secure in their farming operations, that the act is really not for those farmers who could really obtain some value from it.
I want to make a few more remarks on this resolution, Mr. Chairman, so I would ask whether we might call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-103, an Act respecting Atlantic Peat Moss Co. Ltd.-Mousse de Tourbe Atlantic Cie Ltee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I move this bill because it is extremely important for my area, and more particularly for a small village that depends upon the operations of a company. The Atlantic Peat Moss Co. Ltd. has been operating in the Lameque area, in the constituency of Gloucester, for about 15 years and employs an average of 70 people. In 1968, the total amount of the salaries paid was $199,930.
In June last, the Department of Consumers and Corporate Affairs notified the Atlantic Peat Moss Co. Ltd. that it had not filed its annual report. As the head office of the company is in Montreal and the operations were taking place in New Brunswick, the notices could not reach the directors of that company nor the people responsible for that report. The company was dissolved under an act passed by this house.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)

I do not want to give the impression that I am among those who believe that laws are made to be broken. But this company has

October 1, 1968

Atlantic Peat Moss Co. Ltdbeen dissolved and because of the financial implications it is important that it should secure new letters patent. As hon. members know, in the peat moss industry depletion has to be accounted for every year and in this case depletion has gone on for so long that if the company were to apply for a new charter there would need to be a new balance sheet altogether showing an entirely different picture. The working has been depleted for 15 years, so there would only be about 10 per cent of the net value left at this time. speechtext:
I have looked at this bill and I appreciate the comments made by the hon. member with regard to it. It is certainly not in the form of any bill I have previously seen in the years I have spent here. Perhaps because I am not a lawyer the intent of the bill is not very clear to me. I gather either that the company has gone bankrupt or that something else has happened to it leading to a situation which we are asked to correct.
The explanation given by the hon. member also raises a couple of questions. It is not a sponsored measure of the ordinary kind; the hon. member has a healthy interest in it because of the employment aspect. But I am surprised consideration has not been given to some other way of handling what is neither an incorporation nor a renewal of the letters patent. I fail to gather whether the original letters patent were federal or provincial. It would seem to me there are several reasons for handling this matter in another way. We now propose establishing under federal law a company which has to meet several criteria. What we are really doing is this: we are endorsing criteria which were applicable 15 years ago under the letters patent.
I do not necessarily disagree, but I am concerned about the form of redress available to petitioners in cases which must obviously be outside the prerogative of the letters patent office. However, I presume this bill will go to the committee where the question can be discussed further. While I have no objection to this particular case I would certainly not like to see this format used more generally. Widespread use of it would undoubtedly detract from the value of the provisions we have made for letters patent and the right to make decisions with regard to them.
Recently there has been a tendency for more companies to be established by letters patent and fewer by private bills. The trend seems to be reversing in the present instance. No doubt it is worth while to do so since this company is operating in a designated area where 70 employees are dependent upon it. I only hope some consideration will be given to the propriety of this method of relief when relief is not obtainable in any other way. I hope the bill can be sent to the committee for further study at which time those responsible for the administration of letters patent will be in a position to tell us why their legislation was not sufficient to permit what seems to be a simple continuation after default by misunderstanding.

Public Service Staff Relations Act law in order to keep in Canada 51 per cent of the shares.

subtopic: DESIGNATED EMPLOYEES-EXTENSION OF PROHIBITION OF RIGHT TO STRIKE
DESIGNATED EMPLOYEES-EXTENSION OF PROHIBITION OF RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-4, to amend the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when I prepared this bill I did not realize it would come up so quickly. As a matter of fact, I was speaking with the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill before mine on the order paper and I thought he was ready to proceed. I would have liked to have more time but in the circumstances I will proceed anyway.
I might also say that when I filed this bill I did not know I would have the luck to have it drawn so near to the top of the list. I thought it might come up for debate after the Woods commission had reported, but it came up near the top of the draw and the Woods commission is not expected to report until later in the year.
This bill, which proposes changes in the Public Service Staff Relations Act, aims to prevent strikes in the public service where certain public services are essential to the


national economy. Section 79 of the Public Service Staff Relations Act sets out the way in which designated employees are determined. At present that act prohibits the right to strike to designated employees, and designated employees are those:
-whose duties consist in whole or in part of duties the performance of which at any particular time or after any specified period of time is or will be necessary in the interest of the safety or security of the public.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, when parliament passed that act in 1966 it agreed that the right to strike should be limited. It agreed that the right to strike, although it is an important right in a democratic society, was not unlimited and could come into conflict with the public interest. At that time it decided to draw the line at those employees whose duties consisted in protecting the public safety or security.
My proposed amendment would enlarge the area of designated employees. If adopted, designated employees would include not only those whose services are necessary in the interest of the safety or security of the public but also public service employees whose duties consist of services essential to the functioning of the national economy and without which Canada's national and international trade would be seriously impaired. These employees are not defined specifically in my bill, nor are those whose services are considered essential for safety and security.
Under the Public Service Staff Relations Act, when a union asks for certification the public service board first determines whether the employees involved fall within the category of those whose services are necessary for safety and security. Under my amendment it would also have to determine whether the employees concerned fulfil services which are essential to the functioning of the national economy.
What I am doing is not proposing that we take away the right to strike from public servants generally but that we extend the area of designated employees that already exists in the act so that those employees whose services are necessary for the national economy would be considered designated employees, something which would be determined by the board in the same way as the board now makes its determination with respect to other designated employees.
It is my opinion, and the opinion of many other people in this country, that although the right to strike is an essential right in a democratic society it, like all other rights, is
October 1, 1968

not unlimited. All rights can be abused. In civil law we have the theory of "abuse of rights". We also have a principle of democratic society that no private interest should prevail over public interest, over what is good for the public as a whole. When we passed the act in 1966 we accepted that principle and we decided we should have a category of designated employees. Therefore when I voted for the act in 1966 I was convinced at that time that the definition of designated employees in it would be sufficient to protect the public interest.
I was not a member of the committee which studied that matter, although I was very interested in it. As all hon. members know, it is not possible for one to participate in all the committees of the house. At that time I was a member of the consumer affairs committee. It was very active and I could not attend the hearings of both committees. I had to rely on the report that was brought down by the committee dealing with the Public Service Staff Relations Act, which included the present definition of designated employees. Although there was doubt in my mind at that time I voted for the act because I felt that the definition of designated employees would cover all situations necessary to protect the public interest.
All hon. members know that there are many instances where we have to restrict rights, not because it is good but because it is the lesser of two evils. I think this is such a situation right here. I am not dogmatic about this solution, but I say it is in the interest of the public to provide protection against crippling strikes when the public has no means of bargaining and where the employer and the employee, because they cannot reach an agreement, not only hurt themselves in their bargaining process but also to a greater extent hurt the public and may damage the public interest on a long term basis. That interest of the public is paramount, and although the right to strike is a good, desirable right it has to be restricted in certain instances where it produces one of those situations in which you have to chose between the lesser of two evils, the two evils being the abuse of the public interest and the curtailment of the right to strike. As between those two evils, curtailment of the right to strike and abuse of the public interest, we have to draw the line in certain cases, and I propose that we move the line a little farther over than it is at present.

speechtext: The hon. member mentioned the postal strike. Would this apply to all the people who were involved in that strike?

subtopic: DESIGNATED EMPLOYEES-EXTENSION OF PROHIBITION OF RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
No, I do not think it would. There might be employees in any department, for instance, who might be involved in providing safety and security, but not all the employees in the department would be so involved. In other words, it would be a matter for the public service board to determine just as it is now a matter for it to determine. As I have mentioned, in making this proposal I am not suggesting a new principle. The principle already exists in the law. It is just a matter of carrying the principle a little farther because I believe that the present definition in the act is not satisfactory.
During the summer months when we had several strikes in the public area some people called me stating that all strikes in the public service should be outlawed. I cannot agree with that. I feel there are many areas in the public service where a strike would not hurt the public interest. For example, if the employees of the National Film Board, the C.B.C. or many of the civil servants working in more traditional departments went on strike this might not affect the national economy and therefore would not be against the public interest. However, there are areas in respect of which the public service board must be able to determine whether or not the employees should be allowed to strike.
I have mentioned a few areas in the public service where I did not think a strike would be contrary to the public interest and would not harm anyone. Even though the liquor
October 1, 1968

Public Service Staff Relations Act strike in Quebec at the present time is serious and many people are hurt by it, I would not consider this strike to be contrary to the national economic interest of Quebec or the society in which the Quebec liquor board operates, although it has caused a good deal of harm.
On the other hand, however, there are areas in which no one would question that the right to strike should not be allowed. I have in mind police departments, fire departments, the army, and so on. In the middle there are many types of public employee who might be considered to be in a grey area, such as the postal workers, transportation employees, hospital employees, teachers and others. These are areas in which there is a complex question as to whether or not the right to strike should be allowed.
I would hesitate to suggest that we should name in the statutes certain classes of employees. I believe all we can do is set out the principle of the designated employee approach. I think this is the correct approach. The matter is left to the public service board to determine one way or another whether any class of employee falls under the definition. The solution of arbitration as under the present act, of course, is not a perfect one. But in a situation where a strike is very harmful I believe it is the lesser of two evils.
In arbitration a good judgment may be produced, one in respect of which both parties may agree, or there may be a judgment in respect of which one party is satisfied and not the other. On the other hand, I think more is served in the long run by having good arbitration procedures than is served by allowing a strike to continue for a long period with no arbitration procedures or other solution. I have here an editorial from the Montreal Star in which the question of arbitration is discussed. It deals with the recommendations of the Rand report in the province of Ontario. I must say that although I support some of the recommendations in that report I do not support all of them. In commenting on the Rand report the editorial in the Montreal Star of September 7, 1968 states:
A major argument against the creation of the industrial tribunal is that it would be impossible to find the kind of super-geniuses the commissioner envisages for this role. He speaks of tribunal members who would have training and education in political science, economics, sociology, psychology, labour relations, philosophy and history, as well as experience in labour law. This demanding list of qualifications is a correct evaluation of


the complexities involved in industrial relations. But there is a shortage of Messiahs who could fulfil such a role.
The Star editorial is suggesting, in other words, that the type of man necessary to bring about just decisions under compulsory arbitration is not available and because he is not available, therefore we should not have this type of thing. Again I return to the argument I put forward before. In no forum in which we settle disputes are there perfect arbitrators. Even the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada are not perfect men; they are not Messiahs. The men who settle arbitration matters are not Messiahs.
There are situations where a man owns property and the state decides that that property is necessary in the public interest. In this situation the state offers a certain sum of money to the person who owns the property and if that person refuses that sum of money the bargaining is not continued until a price is arrived at. In this type of situation the feeling is that the public interest is paramount and boards are set up to decide what the price should be. A decision is arrived at by the board. The decision may not always be a perfect one. Sometimes the state may not be satisfied. It may feel that the board has granted too great an award for this property. On the other hand, the citizen may feel aggrieved. This situation is felt to be the lesser evil compared with allowing the bargaining process to continue, especially when the public interest is involved.
In answer to the editorial in the Star we say, of course, that there are no perfect judges or arbitrators and there are no perfect members in this parliament. Although we have passed and shall pass laws in this parliament which are not perfect they are the best attempt to deal with certain problems. In areas in which the public interest is involved we must have a system for stopping strikes which are against the public interest. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain), as reported at page 365 of Hansard, delivered a very good speech during the throne speech debate in which he referred to this very subject. He quoted part of a statement made by Walter Reuther, the prominent United States labour leader. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres quoted Mr. Reuther as having said:
It is high time the unions stopped settling their problems at the expense of the community. It is time also for governments to give them such means of settling their problems which will allow them not to depend on strikes alone.

Later in his speech the hon. member quoted figures in respect of strikes in Canada over the last few years. He stated that in 1962 Canada had 290 strikes, that in 1963 we had 318 strikes and in 1964 we had 327 strikes.

In taking this position I do not stand here to say that I like strikes or want strikes to take place, either in the public or the private sector. was coming to that point. I appreciate what the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) has in mind. Although he was a member of the last parliament he was not a member of the committee which went over this bill very thoroughly. I happened to have that privilege, and I am fairly familiar with its terms and the kind of discussion that went into the final decision as to what its terms would be.
As the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) will recognize, the final draft in respect of this area was not precisely what was proposed in the first place. Let me go back behind what the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace was saying, and point out that initially the government said that it was bringing in a bill which would give civil servants the right to strike. When we got the bill we discovered that it was not quite that blank a cheque. On the contrary the right was circumscribed even before we reached the point the hon. member has mentioned. We amended the original provisions so I need not go into all the details, but the way the legislation now reads it provides that a bargaining unit has initially the right to choose between following a course which leads eventually to the right to strike, or to choose to follow a course which leads to arbitration without any right to strike.
I think one of the advantages of a committee was demonstrated in that we got that
October 1. 1968

Public Service Staff Relations Act part of it improved. The original government draft made it necessary for the bargaining unit to make its decision very early in the process, and the decision was binding for quite a long period of time. I forget the exact period but it was binding for longer then we thought necessary.
The government agreed with arguments put forward that this needed to be modified. Thus as it now stands the bargaining unit does not have to make its choice until it gives notice to bargain, and, having made a choice, it applies only for the life of that particular agreement. We think this is an improvement, and I am glad to see the Minister of Labour nodding his head to confirm that the position is as I have stated it.
Thus a bargaining unit of the civil servants has a free choice. It can choose a course that leads to the right to strike or it can choose a course that leads to arbitration. If it chooses the second, it rules itself out of the right to strike at least for that round of collective bargaining.
We went a bit further. We provided that even in the case of those civil servants who elected at the proper time to follow a course that would include the right to strike, that right is limited by a section which says that the unit or the employees in the unit still cannot have that right to strike if their services are such that this would endanger the safety or security of the public.
Let me tell my hon. friend that there were those on the committee who wanted that section worded more broadly or more narrowly, depending on one's point of view. They wanted to put in the general phrase "in the public interest". We in the committee were able to make the point that if you talked about the public interest, the expression is so wide you would remove from everybody the right to strike. So we narrowed it to the terms that are now there. The only people who are denied the right to strike are those whose services are important to the safety or security of the public.
I suggest that Canada is still carrying on, in spite of the strikes we had this past summer. It is good to know, however, that freedom of collective bargaining in labour relations in Canada remains unimpaired. Some of my labour friends might not agree that it has not been impaired to some extent. Generally speaking, however, we still have what we had, and I think this is worth the price we pay in having a few strikes, such as those of the past summer.


The hon. member mentioned strikes in the public area, and I know he is quite interested in the strike that affected the seaway. It is my understanding that the tonnage on the seaway this season will be greater than it was last season, in spite of the strike that took place this year. Statements have been made regarding the grain handlers strike, to the effect that no commitments were lost and that our trade was not really jeopardized. I suggest that the frightening things said about strikes do not always materialize, and that we do have to set over against the harm caused by strikes, the gains that we achieve by maintaining a free society, a free economy, and the right to free collective bargaining.
The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace said he is not against the right to strike but that he wants to balance things. He said further that he is not introducing any new principle in this bill. Let me say to him as strongly as I can that I think this is a dishonest bill. I think this bill actually takes away from our civil servants, once and for all, the right to strike which, within certain limitations, the act has given to them. I have indicated that it is limited already.

speechtext:
suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) read the bill a little more carefully. Remember that already, because civil servants have to make the choice, some deny themselves the right to strike. Remember that for the others this right is, of course, during the term of the collective agreement; but it is provided in the legislation that there cannot be a strike of the unit as a whole, or employees in that unit, if they are involved in work that concerns the safety and security of the public.
If the public service staff relations board had the instruction proposed in this bill, they would say, "There can be no strike because the employees concerned are engaged in work that concerns the safety or security of

the public." But they would also have to say this if the employees' duties consisted of performing services essential to the functioning of the national economy and without which Canada's national or international trade would be seriously impaired. If our public servants are not engaged in work that is essential to the functioning of the national economy, what are we paying them for? All our public servants are engaged in performing services that are essential to our national economy directly or indirectly, and many of them are engaged in performing services that affect Canada's national or international trade.
That is why I say that if you gave the public service staff relations board that kind of instruction, you would be saying to the board, "Take away from all our public servants the right to strike", which was given by the legislation itself. I suppose it is too much to hope that we will hear from him on this subject, but I hope we will. He said some pretty good things about this right when he was handling a couple of strikes with which he had to deal during the first few weeks he was Minister of Labour. As a matter of fact, this is one of the things some of us were complaining about last summer when the postal workers were on strike. A great many people, including many members on the government side, said this was a right they should have. Then they said we must take it away from them. speechtext: The hon. member said my amendment was dishonest because it in fact tried to take away the right to strike. But does he not think the words in the bill would not have this effect? I refer to the words "national or international trade would be seriously impaired". Does the hon. member not think that these words contradict what he says? In other words, this provision would apply to those civil servants whose duties were necessary to the economy, and when you add the words "Canada's national or international trade would be seriously impaired", does the hon. member not think this contradicts what he has said?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: DESIGNATED EMPLOYEES-EXTENSION OF PROHIBITION OF RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
No,
Mr. Speaker, I do not. I am glad the hon. member has quoted me correctly in saying that I think his bill is dishonest, not the author of the bill. You do not modify it by putting in the words "seriously impaired". Remember, of course, that the only people who strike are those who can cause some inconvenience, some dislocation; otherwise there is no point in striking. The strike is part of the process of employees trying to get better wages or working conditions. I suggest in practical terms that any group of public servants who tried to strike under the provisions of the law as it now stands would, if this phrase were included in the law, be met by a board that would have to say, "The work you are doing affects the national economy".
You can say that about any group. This provision would apply to all those whose work affects the national economy or Canada's national or international trade. It does not have to be both; it is "national or international". I do not know how you would define "national trade", but I suppose it means the general trade and commerce that goes on in the country. Certainly the postal workers would have been affected by this provision, as would the grain handlers and the seaway workers. This would also apply to all those classes of public servants who are likely to exercise the right to strike. I am not implying that all these people I have talked about are public servants, but any of them likely to strike would come up against the provisions of this prohibition that the hon. member would seek to write into the legislation.
October 1, 1968

Public Service Staff Relations Act
I agree with the hon. member and all those who say we should find a better way than the strike as a means of solving labour difficulties. But I think those who say we should come up with a better way have an obligation to produce that better way before they take away the one we now have. Arbitration boards have not yet proven to me that theirs is a better way. Perhaps in a few years we will have had some experience in the public service-and mainly that is what we are dealing with here-both ways, because some bargaining units have elected the right to strike and some have elected arbitration. Perhaps we will have some experience and can obtain some advice as to which way to move. But at the moment, until some better way is produced-not just called for, argued for, not just statements that there should be a better way-I do not think it does any service to labour relations in this country generally, and I certainly do not think it does a service to labour relations in the public service, for this kind of legislation to be brought before this house.
It took a long, long time for us to get a government of this country to bring in the kind of legislation that was put into effect during the last parliament. We gave it our endorsation. We should like to have made further changes in it, we would like it to have been even better. But I make no qualification now; it was good legislation. Our public servants are trying to live with that legislation and work it out. They are finding some difficulties with it. But I suggest that at this stage, to say that clamps should be put on it and that certain rights given to our public servants should be taken away is a disservice to the cause of good relations between our public servants and their employees, the government and people of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: DESIGNATED EMPLOYEES-EXTENSION OF PROHIBITION OF RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the speeches that have preceded mine in this debate. I had the privilege of serving in this house in a previous parliament when the first steps were taken toward collective bargaining in the public service. The report of the preparatory committee, to which reference has been made, was certainly one of the basic documents upon which the legislation which is now enacted was eventually constructed.
I know that the joint committee, which held extensive hearings, weighed long and carefully these sections of the act before the

decision was made to incorporate them in the form which has been described. The government of Canada-and I have listened with interest to my hon. friend on the other side- and many members on this side of the house took an active and conscientious interest in promoting what he himself described as a good piece of legislation.
Many members on this side of the house were very much concerned that the government of Canada should act as a good employer. They decided after very careful review that the right to strike should be generally permitted and an exception should be made where very definite reference was made to the safety or security of the people of Canada.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
May I say with the greatest respect to my colleague who introduced this piece of legislation that I do not share his views. I do feel it is important that the legislation which has been introduced should be given a fair period of trial. This it has not had. We are in a formative stage. The very preliminary phases of certification are not completed. There is no question that the process of conclusion of collective bargaining agreements will be a time-consuming one which, I am confident, will bring an entirely different spirit and atmosphere in the public service of this country. I am very reluctant to see anything done at this stage which would disturb what is now being undertaken.
Like other members of this house, this summer I received a number of representations from my constituents. There are those who believe that the postal workers should not have had the right to strike. They argued-and I received a volume of correspondence in this vein-that the right should be proscribed by legislation, and that amendments should be introduced immediately in the house which would have that effect.
There are things that are worse than strikes on occasion. There is no assurance that laws which will prohibit the right to strike will be observed simply because they are laws. During the war when there was a grave danger to national survival we had strikes. Even the severest penalties did not deter men and women under certain conditions from withholding their services on the labour market. Strikes are not always economic strikes, and in general only in economic strikes is the legislation fully protective.
October 1, 1968

There are many other factors behind a strike, and if I may be so bold as to suggest, the strike of postal workers which took place this summer had more to it than met the eye. Behind it was a struggle of groups for leadership of the union, and the rise to the top of one section of the union whose conduct in a previous strike in 1965 had had a singular impact on certain members of the union. There was the question of the relationship of different groups whose prestige was at stake.
I do not believe that a simple prohibition of the right to strike would have assured Canadians that there would have been no strike. But I was very proud of the record of the government of the day, and I am sure hon. members on the other side, and particularly the hon. member who preceded me in this debate, would agree that the conduct of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) in this strike was one of which all Liberal members are proud.
The right to strike was not impaired by precipitous or ill considered action. We regretted the strike very much and it cost many Canadians a price which they could ill afford. However, the strike was eventually resolved within the framework of collective bargaining.
I am one of those who believe that collective bargaining is the best way to resolve these matters. It is sometimes rough, and sometimes irresponsible parties abuse it by resorting to strikes that are ill advised. But the best discipline against it is the discipline of the members of the organization when they realize that they do a disservice to everyone concerned when they resort to a strike which cannot be justified.
Nor do I have that much confidence in the conduct of arbitration boards. The government of this country has had a grave responsibility in setting some kind of pattern which would halt the progress of inflation. A pattern as close as possible to 15 or 16 per cent was indicated as highly desirable. I am not certain that the use of arbitration would have been consistent with the patterns of stability which the government was seeking. There are instances of awards of arbitration boards which have been in excess of the guide lines the government was trying to develop on a voluntary basis. Nor do I have confidence-and the mover of the bill indicated he also had some reservations-that the sort of persons who are chosen to do this farsighted job of applying arbitration and

Public Service Staff Relations Act mediation services have those great talents to judge all the facts which are involved in the circumstances. This calls for skills which very few people possess, and I do not believe that arbitration itself is any guarantee that the other objectives which the government of the day must pursue can be found.
I hope that this bill will receive a long and careful examination by members of this house before it is enacted into legislation.

Mr. Chairman, if I may continue the remarks I was making before the private members hour, there are some broader questions involving credit that I should like to discuss briefly. One of these, which has already been raised in this debate is, what is the effect of credit? No one will argue that the legislation we have had in Canada over the past number of years has not done a lot of good. This legislation has certainly filled some of the yawning gaps that existed in the credit field some years ago. To the extent this has facilitated land transfers, it is really a case of more money chasing the same amount of resources. In so far as this brings about the consolidation of uneconomic farm units, it has produced more efficient farms and has improved over-all productivity. It certainly has helped individual farmers, but it has also contributed to the inflation of land prices. In fact, land prices are skyrocketing in many parts of Canada, and they continue to go up.
I feel I have to take issue with one statement the minister made last night. He is recorded in Hansard at page 600 as stating:
-unrealistic interest rates tend to cause mis-allocation of resources, and in particular terms any savings as a result of a subsidized interest rate on capital borrowed for the purpose of land could make the cost of the land excessively inflationary.

This is, to some extent I suppose, a textbook discussion of the subject. I should like to suggest to the minister that the fact an individual had reasonable interest rates for farm credit over the last number of years has not really contributed to the inflationary spiral of land prices. I should like to suggest that farm needs, technological changes and the availability of credit rather than the cost of credit have, in fact, influenced the initial decisions made by farmers to take advantage of the credit available. Of course we, in our group, are arguing that this does have very significant effects on future costs for farmers. However, I feel it is still true to say that, in many respects, our farmers have no choice but to take advantage of much of the credit that has been available. There is still a good deal of the "next year" philosophy present in farm circles.
The Farm Improvement Loans Act has helped the farmer in the purchase of farm machinery-that is as long as the banks would lend money. The purchase of machinery and equipment generally does improve productivity; but in a situation where machine companies are allowed to set prices on the basis of market forces-and I think it has to be acknowledged that they have had, in some respect at least, something of a monopoly situation-the prices of machinery are bound to go up. The farmer has no choice, really, but to pay the shot if he is going to stay in business. The result has been that the farmer has been caught in this vicious cost-price squeeze. We have had static prices and rising costs. Thus, in spite of higher productivity, farmers have been at a disadvantage. We have had higher costs and lower returns which, in turn, have forced many of our farmers to expand. The only way out of the situation in which they found themselves was the use of larger machinery to carry on their operation. In some cases, after such machinery has been obtained it has been found, as a result of the cost-price spiral, that more land was needed in order to make use of the machinery economic. So, the vicious spiral continues.
Many farmers today are asking if it is necessary for each generation to buy out and repurchase the land they require for their farming operations. It seems to me that some of these problems need to be examined. The government established the Barber commission to investigate farm machinery prices. According to latest information, this report will not be available for some time. In the
October 1, 1968

meantime farmers need machinery. At the moment, they are at the mercy of the machinery companies. If the government is really going to help farmers, they should take action to halt rising machine prices until longer run measures can be developed.
Last winter, Mr. Chairman, in western Canada we heard rumblings from Ottawa that farm credit legislation was receiving a long hard look. This raised the hopes of many people in the west that some new answers would be forthcoming. What happened? On the basis of what we see on the order paper, there are some housekeeping amendments; there is more of what we have had. We are throwing the farmer to the tender mercies of the market, as evidenced by the proposal in respect of interest rates. We do not have a comprehensive approach with regard to credit.
In this regard, it is disappointing to find that we have not tied in the total situation facing agriculture, involving both commercial farms and what might be defined as noncommercial farms. The approach of some people is, of course, that we have to get rid of non-commercial farms. I feel this is a false approach because there are many of these farms that could be helped to achieve an efficient and worthwhile economic status. Essentially, what we need is a different kind of credit for commercial and non-commercial operations. The present program is essentially helping commercial farmers. I feel we do need to have a look at other types of credit that will help what we might define as noncommercial farms.
In addition, we also have the situation facing young farmers which has been dealt with by some of the preceding speakers in this debate. The hon. member for Saskatoon-Big-gar has said we must consider the social consequences of what kind of rural community we are building and helping to encourage by the legislation before us. It is for this reason we need a comprehensive approach toward all aspects of credit needs. I think this makes good economic sense. It makes good social sense.
If this government is really dedicated to priorities, then it must come up with more than what is now on the order paper. No one will quarrel with the claim that the immediate needs have been brought to a crisis point by the dilly-dallying of the Liberal government. However, there is no indication in the legislation, except for one small reference in the minister's remarks, that the government
Farm. Credit Act
is looking beyond the immediate, usual, typical, crisis needs. I hope that this attitude will be forthcoming and that we will have a more comprehensive look at the situation. I urge that the agriculture committee should hold hearings, both in respect of the present legislation and the longer run aspects of farm credit programs, in order that we can better establish the type of credit that is needed and also establish the relationship of credit programs to other farm policies and programs. In this committee, we would bring together specialists and experts, information and experience available in Canada and elsewhere and undertake a thorough study of farmer's needs, in order to arrive at an adequate, sound and far reaching credit program.

Mr. Chairman, now that I have the floor, I would like to express some views about such an important and controversial matter.
I am very happy to have heard the comments of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) beforehand. I must say that I am not convinced of the value of the bill presented by the minister, and instead of trying to establish what priority must be given to finding institutions which will agree to lend money at an unknown interest rate, I feel that it is more important to examine the situation of the farming people and to find other ways to help them.
I would be in favour of looking for ways and means first to guarantee acceptable prices to all farmers and then to determine the possibilities of consumption of our production before thinking of imports.
I wonder whether the most important thing at the present time is to find lending means. Surely it is a worthy undertaking, but it is not a very brilliant measure in the present circumstances.
The bill broadens the classes of persons eligible for loans, and also broadens the purposes for which loans can be made. Those are things which I endorse in principle. However, when it comes to increasing loans from $15,000 to $25,000, when we consider that the rate

of 5 per cent was the maximum rate of interest payable by farmers and that we cannot guarantee a fixed rate for that extension of loans, I wonder how we, who committed ourselves to defending the farming class, who honestly undertook to find solutions to help them, could vote in favour of such a measure without denying our commitments.
Besides, I wonder what would be the situation of those members who agreed with such a proposal. How can anybody honestly vote in favour of such legislation, as I am convinced that all those members representing constituencies with agricultural areas have, like all the others, pledged themselves to fight this interest rate, to help the farmers and to find solutions.
The solution proposed by the Minister of Agriculture does not, under the present circumstances, appear very brilliant or acceptable.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that the loans are a matter for concern. It is certainly possible to help our farmers through the granting of loans, but increasing them will not solve the problem. Loans would simply prolong the present agony of our farmers.
I feel the need is more pressing for means to ensure first of all, decent prices to our farmers. Subsidies are, to my mind, mere band-aids. What our farmers need urgently is for the government to find the means of enabling them to farm their land more profitably.
For instance, I imagine the Department of Agriculture is aware of the April commission report which was submitted to the province of Quebec and which indicated that underground drainage was a priority in that province.
I fail to understand why no one has ever mentioned that the government could put a certain amount of money at the disposal of Quebec; and I imagine that the same problem exists in Ontario where many farmers must have paid the cost of that drainage themselves. I should think that it would be advantageous to allocate certain amounts of money for that underground drainage in the various provinces of Canada which need it, thus enabling our farmers to work on their land earlier in the spring, and later in the fall.

I think this would help our farmers. We might have to come to grants which are only poultices. They are instruments to guarantee prices, and it will only be through co-ordination and planning that we will be able to help

It is certain that, in Quebec particularly, we have diversified farming. This is no reason, I think, not to give each kind of farming the attention it deserves. With regard to the research station established in Quebec under federal jurisdiction and according to a certain plan, I think it would be profitable to find markets to meet the demands of the population and to direct the farmers to those markets where the demand is increasing. In my opinion, these measures would be much more beneficial than trying to find more credit.
I realize that the farmer needs a certain amount of credit, but I do not think we can solve his problems or help him to a better life by lending him more money or by passing a law which would force him to pay a higher rate of interest. As the hon. minister said a while ago, the interest rate af 5 per cent seems unacceptable to him. As for me, I do not honestly think that the farmer is inclined and able to pay more. When considering the situation of the farmers in Canada, I feel sure that we all honestly want to improve the condition of that class of citizens. May I make a suggestion, Mr. Chairman? The Minister of Agriculture recommended a course of action which will have the effect of increasing interest rates to the farmers of this country. Perhaps he more than anyone else here should know that increased interest rates will increase the cost of production. The government should be prepared to follow this credit legislation with a measure respecting farm income and price supports. We are being invited at this time to agree to the suggestion that we squeeze the farmers a little bit harder, as though they have not been squeezed hard enough in the past decade and a half. Does the minister realize that according to the fifth chapter of the report from the Economic Council of Canada our agricultural industry has greater problems than the industry in the United States? Mr. Chairman, I understand there are three resolutions now before the house, one of which will be voted upon in a very few minutes. I shall therefore confine my remarks to the subject matter of this resolution prior to the vote, and continue on with the other two following it.
When the subject of agriculture in any of its forms comes before the house we have to remember two things in looking at the proposed legislation concerning agriculture. One is that agriculture is still by far the largest industry in Canada, and the second is that agriculture is a particularly unique industry for two reasons: One, that it is affected very much by the weather, which is a very important factor because in this country, as we all know, the vagaries of our climate can have a tremendous influence on the crops produced, and the second is that agriculture, because of its very nature, is very much affected by the actions of other governments. I think that while other industries are affected to some degree by the actions of other governments, no industry is affected to the same degree as agriculture, and I will come to this a little later on in my remarks.
I think these two facts are very important and should be borne in mind, because much of the legislation affecting agriculture is regularly misinterpreted by many sections of the public. There is no other industry that is

affected by the weather, and that is as uncertain as is agriculture.
There is perhaps a third factor which must be remembered, namely that it is certainly the responsibility of any government to ensure that the food supply of this country and of certain other countries which rely on Canada is protected.
It is for these reasons among others that very often agriculture has received special consideration in the days gone by. I am referring of course to subsidies, subsidized interest rates and the like. This is very important because of the three rather special factors which do not affect other industries to the same extent. I have heard it said, particularly by those who do not come from farm communities, that farmers are always complaining, and that they always get special attention. speechtext:
A few moments ago, I was discussing the matter of interest rates in connection with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. At that time I indicated that I thought whatever scheme the minister devised for slightly increasing interest rates under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, there will probably be difficulty in obtaining much additional money that way. At the present time, of course, the banks are able to lend most of the money they have available for loans at a much higher rate of interest than the government will be able to provide. The banks will not be worried about security because at the present time they do not seem to be bothering about that aspect of things.
Consequently there is something I hope the minister might take into consideration and that is, instead of increasing the interest rate under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which loans are in the nature of short term or interim term credit, the government might set up a fund similar to the fund it has for the Farm Credit Corporation. In this way, those who borrow under the Farm Improvement Loans Act would know exactly what rate of interest they would be paying. If this arrangement were set up, then the government would not have to rely on the banks to lend money to farmers at whatever interest rate may be decided if the banks decided to lend the money at all.
The farmer would have some assurance of how much interest he would have to pay over the years. I feel that if the government really wants to help farmers with regard to short term loans, the thing to do would be to set up a fund similar to the Farm Credit Corporation fund, and set an interest rate of 5 per cent. When the minister was discussing the Farm Improvement Loans Act he said that some of the functions of this act and those of the Farm Credit Corporation overlapped. He said people could borrow money from a bank under the Farm Improvement Loans Act to make a small purchase of land. Since there is an obvious attempt, apparently, to sort of overlap the arrangements between the Farm Credit Corporation and the Farm Improvement Loans Act, I would think a good way would be to combine the two, put both short term and long term credit under the Farm
October 1, 1968

Credit Corporation. This can be done quite easily by setting up the necessary fund. Then we would not have people going to a bank and finding one branch of the bank turning down a farmer, while another branch said yes. We would get some standardization in this way, as well as lower interest rates.
At the moment, the need for credit of those engaged in agriculture is great. If the government had taken a greater interest in farm policies in days gone by, there would not be the necessity for the extension of credit facilities at this time. Most people do not want to borrow money because it is very difficult to pay it back at the interest rates that are charged now. As I said earlier, I believe the government has a very special responsibility toward agriculture because the government has the responsibility for preserving the country's food supply. We now have a very serious problem in agriculture, and this may very well have a great bearing on the amount of funds available, and the interest rates under this proposed resolution. I refer to the corn problem in Canada.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
This problem is a complex one as most agricultural problems usually are. Very briefly, Mr. Chairman, it is this: First, Canada produces at the present time approximately 70 per cent of its corn needs; the rest comes from the United States of America. Second, the United States government subsidizes in one way or another United States corn growers so that the United States grower receives approximately $1.35 per bushel U.S. funds. Third, the United States grades its corn very differently from the way Canadian grades are rated. This helps what is popularly known as the dumping of corn in Canada. Somebody put it very well when he said that this is "dumping by grading." Fourth, United States corn tends to come into the Canadian market just before the Canadian corn is harvested. Fifth, at the present time the United States government, because of a very large corn crop in the United States, is very anxious to get rid of its stockpiles of corn which it has been piling up for the last year or so. Room is required to store new corn.
Now, Mr. Chairman, remember that the growers in the United States are getting at least $1.35 per bushel as a result of United States government subsidies. This United States corn is dumped on the market in Chicago as low, so I am informed, as 31-cents a bushel. Granted, this is probably very low
679
Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act grade corn, but lots of tricks can be played with the grading of corn.
This, Mr. Chairman, hardly seems fair. Since we import 30 per cent of our com needs, perhaps slightly more, from the United States, the price in the United States tends greatly to affect the price in Canada. I am reliably informed that by the end of this week one of the popular grades of corn in this country will be selling for about $1 per bushel. Corn costs the Canadian farmers an average of $1.22 a bushel to produce. I realize it is difficult to be accurate when talking of averages, but according to the best information I have been able to get, that is the present cost to Canadian corn farmers. If the average price goes down to $1 per bushel, then it is very easy to see what is going to happen to the corn farmers of this country.
Perhaps the government did not foresee this coming, Mr. Chairman, but many com farmers did. A lot of the best corn lands in Canada have been sold in the last short while to what I am informed are wealthy buyers of land from other countries, particularly the United States. These people are purchasing a lot of our best corn lands. I do not think this is an exactly desirable state of affairs. We often complain about our industry, our resources and our lands being taken over by our good neighbours. I do not blame the United States for this; business is business. I blame the government for allowing this sort of thing to happen. If the farmers are forced to sell their corn at $1 a bushel, and perhaps even less before the season is out, since it costs them $1.22 to produce the result will be inevitable.
Dumping is normally understood to be a situation where a country sells its produce abroad at a price lower than it sells it on its domestic markets. Mr. Chairman, this is a piece of fancy fiction. As anyone with experience with dumping duties knows, dumping can be achieved in all sorts of ways-by means of subsidies, direct and indirect, soil banks, special grading of a product, avoidance and evasion of laws, evasion of GATT, and in other ways.
The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that while technically the United States government may not be dumping corn in Canada since it is selling
fact dumping corn in this country, and everybody knows it. This is not the fault of the Canadian farmers. It is not because they are inefficient. It is because the government
680	COMMONS
Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act permits this to happen. The government has very much of a responsibility to protect the people of Canada from this sort of activity. The responsible officials of the Department of Agriculture must have known that this would take place this fall; everybody else seemed to know. However, nothing has been done.
It is the responsibility of this government to protect Canadian citizens from acts of foreign governments. This whole problem, Mr. Chairman, has been caused by the activities of the United States government. I do not blame them. After all, they are only looking after their own people and their own problems. However, their actions affect us. They affect our country and our farmers, who are good and efficient farmers. I suggest that we should not stand for this kind of activity that is depressing the price of Canadian corn.
One argument that has been made, and I think a fallacious one, is that if we cannot produce corn economically in this country, then we should let the corn farmers grow something else. This reminds me of an old expression which was attributed to the unfortunate Queen of France, who said: "If they have no bread, let them eat cake". This of course does not make sense. The United States might not have a surplus of corn next year so there would not be any to dump. In that event, there would be no corn in this country, and this might cause quite a few problems. We cannot rely on the surplus of other countries to furnish our needs. We need an adequate policy in this country to ensure and preserve our food supply. Occasionally we may have to pay for this in the form of a subsidy, but we can spread the payment among the taxpayers. This is small insurance to pay for ensuring that we do not become reliant for food on some other country, and perhaps find ourselves without at some future date. I suggest it is the responsibility of this government to protect our producers from the kind of competition with which they are putting up at the present time.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, quite a bit of U.S. corn is being brought into Canada at prices that, although they vary all the time, tend to be very close to the price presently being paid in Chicago. A lot of people have been wondering who it is who imports this corn into Canada. I do not know who it is. There are some questions on the order paper inquiring into this matter and I hope they will soon be answered, because lots of stories are being circulated. I am not going to say anything more about this, but I think in fairness to all concerned the whole matter

DEBATES	October 1, 1968
should be clarified. I think we should be told who is importing this corn.
Now, Mr. Chairman, since this problem has been presented, we might be asked what are we going to do about it. There have been a number of agricultural organizations in Ottawa the last few days speaking both to members of the government and the opposition. Some of these organizations have suggested that legislation should be quickly prepared to put the corn growers under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. I suggest this would restrict movement of corn. It would certainly stop the importation of this very low cost corn from the United States, it is true, but there are many other disadvantages. Frankly, having discussed the matter with a number of people, I do not think this would be a very good arrangement.
Since time is of the essence, the Canadian corn harvest having now commenced, I think something must be done right away. It is no use the minister saying that various groups of corn growers have different solutions, and when they decide what they want he will give it to them. That is passing the buck. The minister has told us that the people of Canada put this government into office, and I suggest that they expect some decisive action both from the government and from this minister.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I respectfully suggest to the minister that what he should do, since time is of the essence is, by order in council, put corn under the terms of the stabilization act to provide an adequate return to the grower. This could be done quickly. I think he should place it at approximately 115 per cent of the last ten-year average, which would provide a return of approximately $1.39 a bushel to the grower. This will cost the taxpayers money, but it is a small insurance to avoid the problems I referred to earlier. Remember that if the corn growers do go out of business it will put a lot of people out of work. The Cockshutt Co. at Brantford announced the other day that it was letting 500 people go because of lack of demand for farm machinery, arising from uncertainty about markets for agricultural products, including corn. As I say, this proposal will cost some money, but so would extra payments from the unemployment insurance fund. So for Heaven's sake let us keep the farmers in business, give them a proper return for their labours, and ensure the nation's food supply.
October 1, 1968
Since the government is economy minded these days, it might help somewhat if they would try to stop the dumping of cheap corn in this country. This could be done in a number of ways-through discussions with the minister's opposite number in the United States, or perhaps by a suggestion that if no action were taken severe anti-dumping restrictions might be passed. Putting corn under the terms of the stabilization act would be an incentive to the government to try to keep cheap corn out of the country, since to let it in would cost the government money. It would also allay all the fears and uncertainties now present in the minds of corn growers. It would prevent many going bankrupt. It would protect Canadians against unfair competition from abroad. The machinery exists. The action I suggest need only be for a 12-month period; in the next 12-month period the government could possibly find other means of dealing with this problem, perhaps some modification of the Wheat Board arrangement. The government would have time to think of a better solution. Any kind of subsidy should, I think, be only of a temporary nature; but what I have suggested is a good way of doing things, a viable and direct way, and I hope the minister will give it consideration.
