PUBLIC SERVICE-LABOUR DEPARTMENT-STATUS OF WOMEN'S BUREAU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I tried to ask several questions of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) regarding the Women's Bureau in his department, but was ruled out of order. Questions were also asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), but I believe the answers given were not complete. Therefore I put this matter on for discussion tonight.
It was reported yesterday that the Canadian Union of Public Employees announced a brief, which will be submitted to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women this week, stating that the Women's Bureau in the Department of Labour is not doing a proper job in protecting the rights of women as employees.
There were also certain remarks made by Mrs. J. Findlay, who had been director of the Women's Bureau and who retired from that position last February. Both made several criticisms against the bureau, and I can list them as follows. First, they said that the bureau did not have an adequate staff. At present it has only three persons in it. Second, they said that the director did not have enough authority or status, and consequently did not have an important enough role within the Department of Labour. It was suggested that Treasury Board should reevaluate and upgrade the director's position. In this respect there was also criticism that a new director had not been appointed since the retirement last February of Mrs. Findlay. Third, they said that the Female Employees Equal Pay Act passed in 1956, which comes under the Women's Bureau in the Department of Labour, is not adequate, does not

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion have enough teeth, and generally is not sufficient to do what it is supposed to do. Some people have suggested that this act be brought into line with the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and the Fair Employment Practices Act.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The fourth criticism is that the present bureau and the law which it administers is not generally known among women employees. It is suggested that as a consequence women have not taken advantage of the provisions that are already there to protect them. It is suggested further that the bureau should set up an information service to make known to the women the rights they have under the act, which the bureau is in a position to enforce for them. Another suggestion is that the bureau take a more aggressive position with regard to seeking out areas in which women are discriminated against. I might say in respect of the use of more information services, that the story which appeared in the Globe and Mail today was right beside an ad by the Department of Labour Women's Bureau which set out clearly the type of work it does.
I think more should be done in this regard by the Women's Bureau, which comes under the federal Department of Labour. The brief also criticized the lack of communication between the Women's Bureau and other departments within the federal government which deal with matters relating to women. Mrs. Findlay said that although she had certain jurisdiction over many laws which are intended to protect women there was no real communication between her bureau and the other departments of government. She felt that there should be this communication.
The sixth point in the brief is a criticism of the manpower retraining programs in respect of their work among women. I am aware that this does not come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour, but since it is brought up in the brief and is related to labour I think it should be mentioned. It is stated that many women who have been housewives for a long period and who wish to enter the labour force are not able to find employment which would make them productive people in our society.
At present we are not making the most of our female labour force. The Economic Council of Canada has stated that we must take steps to drastically increase our economic production. One certain way of doing this is to have an active, content and highly trained
October 1, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion female labour force. I believe that our women should be given a full role in our economy with men. This will benefit not only the women but also the whole society. I hope that the minister will give careful consideration to the CUPE recommendations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim McNulty (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-LABOUR DEPARTMENT-STATUS OF WOMEN'S BUREAU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks may I say that the minister agrees essentially with many of the observations made in the brief presented to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women by the Canadian Union of Public Employees and re-emphasized this evening by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand).
Statistically, according to the latest figures available, the number of women working in Canada at the end of June 1967 was approximately 170,000. These women are covered by the Female Employees Equal Pay Act or by the provisions of the Public Service Act. At the request of the minister, shortly after he took office a review of the Women's Bureau was made as well as an appraisal of the act to which I have just referred. Steps were immediately taken to fill the vacant role of director of this important branch and to upgrade its classification to bring it more in line with the degree of importance that the minister attaches to this area of his department. As a result of this study, a director has been chosen at a classification and salary that is in line with those paid to other branch heads. The name of this director will be announced very shortly, provided of course that there are no appeals against her choice as permitted under the Public Service Act.
While I am sure all members realize that federal jurisdiction extends to a comparatively limited number of women in the work force of Canada, it is realized that the federal department has a responsibility to lead rather than follow the provinces in recognition of the growing importance of women in the labour force, and to do everything in its power to eliminate all forms of discriminatory practices.
As the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace has pointed out, the Female Employees Equal Pay Act is basically good legislation. Its weakness rests with the fact that it acts only on complaints brought to our attention by affected workers. Perhaps as Mr. Little of the union pointed out, we have not made sufficient efforts to acquaint women with this act and its provisions. Perhaps the unions have been lax as well in not acquainting their

membership with the provisions of the act; but indeed Mr. Little was frank and honest enough to indicate that the unions themselves are not without blame.
Proposed changes to the act have been suggested to the minister, but it is hoped that these changes can be reviewed when the report of the royal commission is changed, in order that the act be made as perfect as possible.
It is obvious, for instance, that the proposed changes must permit the department to initiate action and determine whether or not discrimination is being practiced against the female segment of our working force. If past history is any indicator, provincial legislation usually follows shortly afterwards.

maintopic: OIL-REPORTED REDUCTION IN U.S. IMPORTS FROM CANADA
OIL-REPORTED REDUCTION IN U.S. IMPORTS FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I asked two questions of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The first one was, briefly, did the United States make a unilateral decision to cut back the quotas on exports of crude petroleum from Alberta, Canada, to the United States, or was this the result of negotiation between the two countries. I received an answer which gave statistical information about what has happened in the past. I am not talking today about what has happened. I then put this question to the minister:
Perhaps the minister did not quite understand my question. We all realize that the national oil policy is subject to negotiation, but did Canada negotiate this export loss in crude petroleum to the United States or was this done on a unilateral basis by the United States?
I have discussed this matter with the top people in the oil industry and they advise me there has been a cutback for the next quarter of 10,000 barrels of crude per day. As a result of that situation the Calgary Herald of September 28, 1968 carried the following heading: "Alberta oil exports cut" and the subheading "U.S. to restrict imports". This article was written by Fraser Perry, one of our more reliable newspapermen, who thoroughly understands this particular subject.
I wanted to obtain an answer from the minister as to whether this cutback had been negotiated, or is the result of unilateral action by the United States. I was not being critical of the government.
October 1, 1968

The article to which I referred reads in part as follows:
United States action which could cost Alberta export sales totalling close to 10,000,000 barrels of crude oil in the next three months, has created new tensions in Ottawa, Washington and the oil centres of North America.
This is causing tension as well in Calgary, the oil capital. The oil industry has stated without reservation or equivocation that there has been a cut-back. I am not denying or arguing for one moment that since the implementation of a national oil policy in 1961 there have been negotiations, or that the National Energy Board set up by the Conservative government has done an excellent job in this regard. Neither am I denying that in the last three months there was an improvement in the export of oil. What I am saying is that now there is a cut-back.
Several months ago when I suggested there was a cut-back in the export of grain the former government practically laughed me out of the House of Commons. This government has statistics which show what a great job it is doing in this field, and I am not denying that. What I am saying now is that it does not make any difference whether you have statistics or not, if representatives of the industry were in my place tonight they would tell you that the maximum exports we have ever had represent only 30 per cent to 40 per cent of our production.
The Canada Year Book, which I think is pretty reliable, indicates that we import crude petroleum into eastern Canada through the Montreal market to the extent of 395,000 barrels of crude oil per day from Venezuela, Arabia, Iran and Iraq. We export to the United States-I say "we", but it is American capital that is bringing the crude petroleum in here-on an average only 295,000 barrels of crude petroleum daily. A few days ago this figure was cut by 10,000 barrels.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
It is obvious that the minister did not negotiate on behalf of Canada; it is obvious that it was a unilateral deal. I say this is obvious because the minister would not answer the question today. He wanted to give statistics on what had been done in the last three months. I am not questioning his figures; he and I can give figures. But as of today we have lost the export of 10,000 barrels per day from the Calgary area. This is the seriousness of the situation. The industry has pointed this out. I do not think the minister
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion would argue with the newspapermen, companies in the United States and the industry in Canada; surely he will not do that.
I have here some figures which were obtained from the National Energy Board. In the first quarter of 1968 the industry in Calgary exported 293,000 barrels of crude petroleum per day to the United States. In the third quarter of that year the figure was
353,000	barrels per day. But there has now been a cut-back to 280,000 barrels per day, which is less than the average mentioned in the Canada Year Book. This is less than the average last year, and there is definitely a fall-off.
In addition, Mr. Udall, the minister of the interior of the United States, has advised the industry in the United States that they must cut back on their imports of crude petroleum from this country. That is only a suggestion from the government in Washington, but as my good friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) appreciates, when they get a suggestion like that, they take it as an order.
In the Puget Sound area, which is the Washington-Vancouver area, 140,000 barrels of crude petroleum per day go in. That figure is being cut back to 100,000 barrels per day. Because of this situation I sought information from the minister today as to what the government is doing about it. I wanted to know whether they were negotiating with the United States. Are they saying to the United States, "You have the Montreal market. You refine crude petroleum. You bring in 395,000 barrels of crude petroleum per day, and that finds its way into refined products that are sent to Toronto and even farther west." This is the area which was negotiated between Canada and the United States and is our western supply centre.
So basically we are in this position: We are losing our domestic market and our exports. We want to keep up our gross national product, but the same thing will happen in western Canada with regard to petroleum as happened with grain. This government said they would give western Canada representation, and they would give some power to the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatchewan and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) from Alberta. It is true they are now members of the cabinet, but they are being stripped naked of their jurisdiction and powers in this government. That is our complaint, and we are trying to get information from the minister.
October 1, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I repeat that I am not quibbling about whether the figure was 117,000 barrels, but I am saying there has now been a cutback. I want to know whether this was a unilateral or a negotiated arrangement. If it was a negotiated arrangement, why did Canada give in to the United States?

POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-RECONSIDERATION OF POLICY RESPECTING RURAL MAIL CONTRACTS
POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-RECONSIDERATION OF POLICY RESPECTING RURAL MAIL CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, September 27, the Postmaster General in a brief statement to the house announced the curtailment of mail deliveries starting on February 1. The key sentences in this statement which appeared at page 496 of Hansard were the following:
Deliveries of mail will not be made on Saturdays. This will include letter carrier service, parcel post and rural route deliveries.
This gives rise to any number of questions, but these are at least three of them: The hardship on those expecting six day mail delivery; what happens to the working conditions of the mail carriers; and the particular subject of this inspiring debate, namely what effect it will have on the rural mail carriers. And of course the public interest must also be considered.
My own question to the Postmaster General, among the many being put to him today, refers to the formula that would be used to achieve new contracts with rural mail carriers who have had capital expenditures on their automobiles, as a rather necessary and basic part of their contract. The Postmaster General's answer to other questions was that he was not willing to spend six days money for five days service. I would point out to him that there is a capital investment in a car. While the minister can order the rural mail carriers to deliver five days a week instead of six, he cannot stop the depreciation on the car. It will continue from one week to another.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I believe the minister will agree with me, and I think most members will agree with me, particularly those in rural or partial rural
October 1, 1968

constituencies, that the rural mail carrier does not have a happy life. He is usually in competition with somebody else before he can get a contract to deliver the mail. He usually pares the cost as close to the line as he possibly can-and sometimes goes below it, because after a period of two years these contracts are almost always renegotiated with the department itself. The rural mail carrier must take his chances on a rise in the cost of automobile licences or a change in the rate of car insurance. These things can make a very substantial difference in that gentleman's financial position.
In so far as the car itself is concerned, he has to meet monthly payments. My experience, and I dare say this has been the experience of many other members, has been that the financing of cars gives rise to more legal problems for the people across Canada than anything else. I hope therefore that in paring costs or cutting down the deliveries from six days to five, some heed will be paid by the Postmaster General and his department to the capitalization of the vehicle, whether it be a bright and shiny car or some old heap driving Her Majesty's mails down the highways and byways of this nation.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-RECONSIDERATION OF POLICY RESPECTING RURAL MAIL CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) and myself are at odds on this question at all. I simply said, in reply to his question this afternoon, that obviously the contracts will have to be renegotiated. I recognize the points the hon. member has brought out, that the mail carrier is faced with certain fixed costs such as depreciation whether he works five days or six days. These costs are not going to be reduced, nor are his insurance charges. Obviously any renegotiation of the contracts will take account of these facts.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
On the other hand, the mail carrier will not be working six days a week. He may or may not be in a position to find other employment on Saturday or over the week end. The point is we certainly should not allow the contracts to stand as they are because the direct, out of pocket expenses such as gas and oil and all the rest will not be expenses for that Saturday. Obviously there is room here for renegotiation. There is room for taking account of the public interest and the responsibility of the minister to act wisely as a trustee of the public funds which are placed at his disposal. There is room here for reasonable renegotiation, with all that word may imply.
As I suggested, the Post Office Department and the government are sensitive to the fact that a great many mail contractors are not gaining an adequate living. This fact raises other problems, such as whether we should not-we are doing it, by the way-conduct a complete re-examination of the rural routes as they presently exist to ascertain if it is not possible, when two contractors side by side make $3,000 or $4,000 a year each, to amalgamate the two routes and thus assure one rural mail carrier of a reasonable living.
All of these questions are to be included in a general re-examination by the department, and this examination is going ahead very rapidly. We recognize all this, Mr. Speaker, and in the bill to come down I think the hon. member will also find we have taken account of it. With regard to the precise problem he has raised, that of depreciation, we may even make some suggestions about longer contracts that will provide for a better depreciation of the contractor's equipment.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.28 p.m.
